gao-gaoreports-gao-08-252: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at homeland Defense: Steps Have Been Taken to Improve US Northern Command's Coordination with States and the National Guard Bureau, but Gaps Remain. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-452: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at medicare Part B Imaging Services: Rapid Spending Growth and Shift to Physician Offices Indicate Need for CMS to Consider Additional Management Practices. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-52: GAO told the Air Force in 2007 to write real rules for buying and running its business software. The service was spending big on finance and supply programs with no firm playbook for picking winners. The report targets a classic Pentagon trap: billion-dollar tech buys launched on hope, then nursed along long past the point of no return.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-852: GAO published its findings on homeland Security: DHS Risk-Based Grant Methodology Is Reasonable, But Current Version's Measure of Vulnerability is Limited in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
goodwin-graeco-egyptian-magic-1852:
Charles Wycliffe Goodwin published the first English rendering of a Greek magical papyrus in 1852. His edition presents papyrus PGM V from the British Museum's Anastasi collection. Greek text, English translation, and notes appear together in the volume.

The papyrus holds a working handbook of spells from Roman Egypt. Love charms, dream-sending rites, and prayers to Egyptian gods fill its columns. Goodwin, an Egyptologist and judge, recognized the text's importance early. His edition opened serious study of ancient magic to English readers. Historians of religion still treat the publication as a landmark. The spells mix Greek and Egyptian traditions freely.
guillaume-clerc-bestiaire-divin-hippeau-:
Guillaume le Clerc, a Norman poet, wrote the Bestiaire divin around 1210. It is a bestiary in French verse, each beast matched with its Christian meaning. Hippeau's edition of 1852 supplies this text of the great thirteenth-century poem.

Guillaume treats lion, unicorn, pelican, and dozens more in rhyming lines. He describes each creature's nature, then draws the lesson for the soul. His verse is graceful, and his morals are aimed at ordinary hearers. The poem stands among the finest of the verse bestiaries. Hippeau's careful edition kept it available to scholars. Together, poem and edition preserve a high point of medieval animal lore.
gulistan-eastwick-1852:
Edward B. Eastwick published his English Gulistan in 1852, the first translation of Saadi's Rose Garden into prose and verse together. Saadi of Shiraz wrote the Gulistan in Persian in 1258, after a lifetime of travel and study. Eastwick adds a life of the author drawn from the Atish Kadah.

Kings, dervishes, schoolboys, and wrestlers pass through eight chapters of tales and maxims. Each short story lands on a line of counsel about mercy, contentment, speech, or power. Saadi mixes prose with verse morals in the Persian manner, and Eastwick follows him. Persians have quoted the Gulistan for seven centuries as their handbook of wisdom. Eastwick's pioneering version opened it to the English world.
hahnemann-lesser-writings-1852:
Samuel Hahnemann wrote far more than the Organon, and The Lesser Writings of 1852 gathers that scattered work in one place. R. E. Dudgeon edited the volume, with notes by Richard Hughes. Essays, letters, and case notes sit side by side, spanning Hahnemann's long career as the founder of homeopathy and its first arguer.

Some pieces argue with critics, while others record single cures or early drug trials. Together they show his ideas forming well before the famous system took shape. Students who know only the Organon find a fuller Hahnemann here: sharper, more restless, and always testing his rules against practice.
hawthorne-blithedale-romance-1852:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Blithedale Romance in 1852, his novel of a utopian farm community. The book is a roman à clef of Brook Farm, where Hawthorne had lived in 1841. It is the first great American novel of utopian community and its discontents in fiction.

Poet Miles Coverdale, the narrator, spies on his fellow reformers from trees and hermitage hides in Blithedale. Hollingsworth, a stern prison reformer, bends the commune to his single driving cause of reforming criminals. Zenobia, proud and passionate, and meek Priscilla fall into a triangle that ends in river death. Coverdale's voyeur gaze makes him the least trusted teller Hawthorne ever built into a tale here. The book asks if reformers love mankind or only their own grand schemes.
hugo-napoleon-the-little-1852: Napoleon the Little, Victor Hugo's 1852 denunciation. The tyrant unmasked. This book preserves that polemic. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The text survives intact.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstein-leop:
Leopold Löwenstein, a German rabbi born in Gailingen, Baden, on December 1, 1843, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer. He studied at the gymnasium at Bischofsheim and learned Talmud from his father, a district rabbi. He then attended the University of Würzburg and the yeshivah of Rabbi Israel Hildesheimer at Eisenstadt.

In 1872 Löwenstein became district rabbi in his native place, and in 1887 he moved to Mosbach, Baden, serving three districts from there. He was decorated in 1891, and the article lists his histories of the Jews at Lake Constance and in Germany. Since 1900 he had also edited a journal supplement on Jewish history and literature. The entry captures a working rabbi who doubled as a local historian, and it names the books where his research can still be found.
king-henry-iv-part-2-pg2252: "I know thee not, old man" falls like a hammer in this edition: the new King Henry V casts off Falstaff at his coronation. The tavern's laughter dies as the crown's weight settles. The saddest of the histories, farewell to all follies.
kircher-oedipus-aegyptiacus-vol1-1652:
Athanasius Kircher attempts to read the hieroglyphs in Oedipus Aegyptiacus, Volume One, in Latin from 1652. Obelisks in Rome supply his texts, and Coptic his hoped-for key. Kircher got the details wrong, yet in trying he founded the serious study of ancient Egypt for the European world of his age.

Hundreds of engravings make the work a feast for the eye. Gods, rites, and symbols of Egypt fill its vast, learned pages. Jesuit missions fed his cabinet with reports from three continents here. The book stands as baroque scholarship at its most splendid, magnificent in scope even where its readings miss the mark entirely.
las-casas-brevisima-1552:
In 1552 Las Casas printed his Brevísima relación, a short account of ruin in the Indies. The Dominican friar addressed his sharp tract to the Spanish court itself. He meant to shock Spain into changing how it ruled the New World.

Page by page, he lists massacres, forced labor, and whole peoples wiped out. The style is brief, blunt, and built for outrage and action. Read at court and printed across Europe, the tract spread fast. It changed how Europe judged the Spanish conquest for good. Many still call it the most telling protest pamphlet ever written.
maidstone-six-witches-1652:
Six women were condemned at the Maidstone assizes in 1652, and their story was sold as A Prodigious and Tragicall History. The Kent trial ranks among the major witch cases of the Interregnum, the years when England had no king. The pamphlet gives the charges and the court's sentences.

Its title sells wonder and sorrow at once, and the text inside keeps that tone. Readers learn who the six were, what harm was laid to them, and how the court dealt with each. The case shows the witch trial alive and well under the republic. Print and panic still walked hand in hand in 1652.
newman-idea-of-university-1852:
When Newman became rector of a new Catholic university in Dublin, he gave the lectures published in 1852 as The Idea of a University. They define what a university is for, beyond training for jobs or trades. The book became a foundational text of Christian higher education.

Newman argues that knowledge is its own end, and that a liberal education trains the mind to think clearly and whole. He also defends a seat for theology among the sciences, since each field of study needs the others to stay honest. College teachers still quote his lectures in fights over what schools owe their students.
openalex-w1985061352: The Chagas bug was supposed to stay in the wild. A 2008 genetics study by Fitzpatrick and colleagues revealed that wild Rhodnius prolixus do colonise rural houses in Venezuela. The finding challenged four decades of vector control assumptions.
openalex-w2059134652: Chagas parasites swap powerhouse DNA. A 2012 study revealed mitochondrial mixing events in Trypanosoma cruzi with deep sequencing of mitochondrial rings. The work rewrote the parasite's genetic history — the family tree changed for good and all.
openalex-w2115545952: Water science needs volunteers. A 2014 paper explores crowd science in water science. The work mapped chances for new knowledge, ecosystem care, and sustainable development — the public as helpers, welcome to the mission ahead, worldwide.
openalex-w2922176752: Species are shifting fast, and conservation needs reliable, integrated data to respond. This 2019 Nature Ecology & Evolution paper develops essential biodiversity variables for mapping and monitoring species populations. The framework guides the policies meant to sustain nature's functions and benefits.
openalex-w2925057452: Flooded soil suffocates plants — but submergence and waterlogging stress them differently. This 2019 Frontiers in Plant Science review highlights research opportunities and understudied aspects of how plants cope with too much water. On farmland and in nature alike, the review argues, flood tolerance deserves more attention.
openalex-w2956483952: Humanity needs a clean, resilient, productive, and well-observed ocean — 'the ocean we need for the future we want.' This 2019 Frontiers in Marine Science paper makes the case for the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development. The proclamation rallies the world to study and steward the seas.
openalex-w7125686452: Heart failure already limits life; anemia makes it worse. This study of Pakistani patients measured how low red blood cells affect daily functioning in chronic heart failure. The authors quantified the added burden. A clinical study of two burdens compounding.
openalex-w7128725752: A crystal of europium makes odd electricity from magnetism. This lab paper reports a strange sideways voltage in EuTi2Al20, where europium atoms form a diamond-like grid, near its magnetic flip points. The team measured the effect near absolute zero. A study of magnets making their own power.
ovid-heroides-amores-art-riley-1852:
Henry T. Riley turned Ovid's early love poems into English prose for Bohn's library in 1852. The volume gathers four works of the young Ovid: the Heroides, the Amores, the Art of Love, and the Remedy of Love. Together they made Ovid the teacher of love for the Roman world and for ages after.

The Heroides are letters from mythic heroines, Penelope, Dido, and Medea among them, to the men who left them. The Amores chase a mistress through Rome in witty elegies. The Art of Love then gives mock-serious rules for winning and keeping a lover, and the Remedy cures the wound. Riley's prose keeps the sense plain for students.
plos-pbio-0020152:
Paolo Norio and Carl L. Schildkraut studied how a virus copies its DNA in PLOS Biology in 2004. Epstein-Barr virus lives in human cells as small DNA rings called episomes. Each ring must be copied once per cell cycle, from start points that can shift.

The team found that where copying starts on the ring is flexible, a trait called plasticity of initiation. The virus does not depend on one fixed start site. That freedom may help it persist in many cell states without failing to copy. Epstein-Barr virus is tied to several cancers, so its copying rules matter. Knowing them can point to weak spots in how the virus maintains itself.
plos-pbio-0020352:
Jeb Gaudet, Srikanth Muttumu, Michael Horner, and their team charted gene activity in the early gut in PLOS Biology in 2004. The foregut gives rise to organs like the liver, lungs, and pancreas. Using the worm C. elegans, the team read gene activity across the whole genome as the foregut formed over time.

The time series shows waves of genes switching on in order, each wave preparing the next stage. Many of those genes match ones used in our own gut organs. A simple worm thus gives a timed script for a process that is hard to watch in mammals. The data set serves labs that study organ birth defects and stem cell work aimed at growing gut tissue.
plos-pone-0000052:
Raúl de la Fuente-Fernández weighed a hopeful idea about Alzheimer's disease in a 2006 paper: if doctors could protect nerve cells, neuroprotection, would fewer people develop the disease? Alzheimer's incidence, the rate of new cases, rises steeply with age, and no treatment then could prevent it. Prevention was the prize.

His analysis considers the impact neuroprotection could have on incidence, reasoning from what is known about how the disease develops over years before symptoms. Even delaying onset changes the arithmetic of an aging population, since many would die of other causes first. The paper makes that population-level case, a style of argument that now anchors Alzheimer's prevention planning.
plos-pone-0000152:
Raffaele Vardavas and Sally Blower published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It looks at Botswana, where HIV treatment programs had expanded, and asks when transmitted drug resistance would pass the World Health Organization's detection threshold. Transmitted resistance means new infections already carry virus that resists first-line drugs.

As treatment scales up, some resistance is expected to spread; the question is how fast. The authors model the rise of resistant virus in the population. Their timing estimate helps treatment programs plan surveillance, so resistance gets spotted by testing rather than by watching patients fail therapy.
plos-pone-0000252:
Guangcheng Zhang, Amir H. Assadi, Robert S. McNeil, and colleagues published this neurobiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reelin is a signal that guides young neurons to their places in the developing brain, acting through a receptor called VLDLR. The authors show that the Pafah1b complex, tied to the brain disorder lissencephaly, interacts with that receptor.

When brain layering goes wrong, as in lissencephaly, children face severe disability. Connecting Pafah1b to the Reelin pathway joins two lines of evidence about how layers form. The paper helps explain how migrating neurons read their directions during development.
plos-pone-0000352:
Roy R. Chaudhuri, Chuan-Peng Ren, Leah Desmond, and colleagues published this bacterial genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genome sequencing of European isolates of Francisella tularensis subspecies tularensis, the tularemia bacterium, shows a surprise. They are almost identical to the US laboratory strain Schu S4, a strain kept in labs for decades.

Wild strains from Europe matching an old lab strain so closely is odd for a bacterium. It hints that this subspecies changes very slowly and spread only in recent times. Tularemia is a watched disease, so its family history matters when tracing outbreaks.
plos-pone-0000452:
Anthony I. Jack and colleagues charted how the brain's visual territory is organized, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Vision begins in early visual cortex, at the back of the head, and spreads forward into extra-occipital regions that handle faces, places, and objects. The team studied changing human visual field organization along that route.

A visual field map records which part of what you see each patch of cortex handles. As maps change from early to later areas, they reveal how the brain trades precise geography for meaning. Understanding that organization underlies work on vision loss and on how the brain rebuilds the world from the eye's signals.
plos-pone-0000552:
Patrick S. Sullivan and colleagues studied why some HIV patients skip their medicine, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Antiretroviral therapy works only if taken consistently; missed doses let the virus rebound and develop resistance. The team identified patient and regimen characteristics associated with self-reported nonadherence to therapy.

Knowing who struggles, and with which kinds of regimens, lets clinics target support instead of blame. Simplifying regimens and matching them to patients' lives are practical responses. Adherence research of this kind quietly determines whether powerful drugs deliver their trial results in the real world.
plos-pone-0000652:
Létitia Jean, Benjamin Thomas, Abdessamad Tahiri-Alaoui and colleagues revisited a suspect enzyme in Alzheimer's disease for PLOS ONE in 2007. Diseases of abnormal protein folding need an initial trigger, which may be infectious, inherited, inflammatory, or unknown. Cutting proteins into vulnerable pieces, such as the amyloid-beta peptide, can start the aggregation.

Their angle is heterologous amyloid seeding, one protein's aggregates seeding another's. They ask what role acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme long tied to Alzheimer's, plays in that seeding. The question revisits an old player with a new mechanism in mind. If one aggregate can seed others, the spread of damage in the brain reads differently.
plos-pone-0000752:
Andy Gardner, Stuart A. West and Ashleigh S. Griffin asked whether a survival trick in bacteria counts as social behavior. Antibiotic resistance by mutation is well reported. Less known are persister cells, which resist antibiotics not by inheritance but by switching to a slow-growing state that drugs cannot kill. Within one population, only some cells make that switch.

If persisters protect their relatives by outlasting treatment, persistence could be a social trait maintained for the group's sake. Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper tests that framing. The answer shapes how doctors think about relapsing infections, and how evolution explains cells that seem to sacrifice growth for the colony.
plos-pone-0000852:
Jianing Wei, Lizhong Wang, Junwei Zhu and colleagues showed that plants call in wasp bodyguards with a specific scent chemical, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plant volatiles play an important role in defending plants against insect attacks by attracting their natural enemies. Green leaf volatiles and terpenoids emitted from herbivore-damaged plants were known to help parasitic wasps locate hosts, the caterpillars the wasps lay eggs in.

Their title narrows the signal: plants attract parasitic wasps by releasing hexenol, one green leaf volatile. A single named molecule makes the defense testable and usable. Farmers could one day spray hexenol-like signals to summon wasps instead of spraying insecticide.
plos-pone-0000952:
Wolfgang Forstmeier asked whether female birds differ in their own readiness to mate outside the pair, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Extra-pair paternity is common in wild birds, and many studies count how often it happens. Much less is known about whether individual females have a stable personal tendency toward it.

Forstmeier separates the female's own propensity from the push of circumstance. If readiness is a lasting trait, it could evolve like any other. If it is mostly situation, then opportunity rules. The question reframes a familiar field result: behind every extra-pair brood sits a female decision, and those decisions may not be equal.
plos-pone-0001052:
Ansar Pathan, Clare Sander, Helen Fletcher and colleagues tested boosting the TB vaccine with a modified virus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. BCG is the standing tuberculosis vaccine, and its protection fades. The booster candidate, MVA85A, is a modified vaccinia virus carrying a TB antigen called 85A.

The team investigated the safety and immune effects of giving the boost shortly after BCG. They compared results with BCG alone and with an earlier trial using a longer interval. Timing can make or break a booster, since the first vaccine's response is still rising. Their comparison helps set the schedule for larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0001152:
Some macaques infected with SIV, the monkey relative of HIV, keep the virus under tight control. John Loffredo and colleagues studied these elite controllers in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Killer T cells are widely accepted to play a key role in holding immunodeficiency viruses down.

The team showed that CD8 T cells from the controller monkeys recognize viral pieces presented by a molecule called Mamu-B*08. They also tracked how the virus varied under that immune pressure. Work like this parallels human studies of HIV control and informs what a vaccine would need to achieve.
plos-pone-0001252:
When yeast cells meet DNA-damaging agents, they switch on a massive program of gene activity. Ivan Rusyn and colleagues sorted out which part of that program answers DNA damage specifically, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The complication is that damaging agents also harm other cell components, proteins and membranes included.

The authors studied transcriptional networks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae linked to an accumulation of intermediates from base excision repair, the pathway that fixes small DNA lesions. By tying gene responses to those repair intermediates, they isolate the DNA-specific signal. The work clarifies how cells sense and answer genome damage.
plos-pone-0001352:
Paramecium bursaria is a single-celled organism that carries several hundred green algae living inside itself. Toshiyuki Takahashi and colleagues studied its internal streaming, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The cell shows rotational, microtubule-based cytoplasmic streaming. Granules and the symbiotic algae flow in a constant direction. Why the flow matters was unclear.

The authors report that arrest of cytoplasmic streaming makes the algae multiply in the green paramecia. Stop the flow, and the resident algae grow fast. That coupling suggests the host uses streaming to manage its tenants. It is a neat finding about how the two partners live together.
plos-pone-0001452:
Jo Fleming and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on blood vessel loss in scleroderma. In this immune ill, harm to small vessels drives much of the disease burden. The team used stains and gene readouts to chart vessel state in patient tissue. They asked whether stem cell care can grow vessels back.

Their data explore whether treated patients show signs of new vessel growth. They also weigh whether the disease traits can in part reverse. Small vessel repair would be a real shift for a disease with few good options. The study gives a base for larger trials of stem cell care in scleroderma.
plos-pone-0001552:
Geoffroy Berthelot and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the arc of world records in sport. Records show the top edge of human speed and strength. The team charted how records have risen over time and what shaped that rise. Past gains had come in a near steady climb.

Their charts show the climb now bends toward a flat top. They read this as the close of a brief era of peak gains. Wars, drugs, gear, and wealth all left marks on the curve. A flat top would shift sport's focus from raw records to other forms of contest.
plos-pone-0001652:
Rulong Shen, Yin Ye, Li Chen, and their co-authors asked where the blood vessels inside tumors come from, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tumors need new vessels to grow, invade, and spread. Most accounts credit angiogenesis, in which nearby vessels sprout into the tumor. But tissue studies had hinted that tumor cells themselves might seed the vessel lining.

The team worked with precancerous stem cells, cells that are not yet full cancer but are on the way. Their results support the idea that such cells can act as progenitors for tumor vessels. The full text gives the cell markers, the vessel structures they formed, and the tumor tests. If tumors build part of their own blood supply, drugs that only block vessel sprouting may miss a route of growth.
plos-pone-0001752:
Usha Chinappen-Horsley, Glen M. Blake, Ignac Fogelman, and their co-authors hunted genes for bone length in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Human height is highly heritable but complex, and finding its genes had proven harder than expected. One reason may be that height lumps many bone lengths into one noisy measure.

Using DEXA imaging, which measures bones precisely, in the Twins UK cohort, the team ran a genome-wide linkage scan for bone lengths. They report quantitative trait loci on chromosome 5. The full text gives the twin data and the linkage peaks. Measuring single bones instead of total height is a cleaner way to find the genes that build the skeleton.
plos-pone-0001852:
Federica Chiara and co-authors studied a sugar burning enzyme's role in cancer cell death in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Type II hexokinase is made in excess in most tumor cells and mainly sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane. Its release from mitochondria triggers apoptosis, the cell's self-kill program. The standard model held that its contact with voltage-dependent anion channels kept cells alive.

The team reports that hexokinase II release triggers apoptosis through the permeability transition pore, without needing voltage-dependent anion channels. The full text gives the cell tests. Changing the model matters because drugs built to pry hexokinase off mitochondria are a live cancer plan.
plos-pone-0001952:
Jinhong Hu and co-authors ran a first human safety test of a malaria vaccine in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The vaccine is built from a fused protein that joins parts of two proteins from the malaria parasite, AMA-1 and MSP-1. In rabbits and monkeys, the fused protein raised antibodies that block the parasite.

The phase one trial gave the vaccine, mixed in an oily carrier called Montanide ISA 720, to healthy adults. It was randomized, partly blinded, and used a dummy dose for comparison, with doses raised in steps. First trials like this check safety and immune response before any test of real protection.
plos-pone-0002052:
John Lin and co-authors mined six years of neuroscience meeting abstracts, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Annual meeting abstracts from scientific societies hold rich arrays of information about a field. The team extracted and processed abstracts presented at the Society for Neuroscience meetings from 2001 to 2006.

By computing over titles and text at scale, they aimed to distill the state and dynamics of neuroscience. They tracked what topics rose, which faded, and how the field's language shifted. Abstract mining of this kind turns a yearly flood of talks into a map a whole field can read about itself.
plos-pone-0002152:
Jae Myoung Suh, Drew Stenesen, John Peters, and co-authors hunted for genes that control lifespan in the fruit fly, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fat-storing tissue has been shown to sway how long flies live. The team used a screen in the fly's fat body, inserting genetic switches to find genes that change longevity.

Their screen turned up a sorting nexin, a protein that helps route cargo inside cells, carrying a domain tied to signals that switch genes off. The find links the cell's internal sorting work to the pace of aging. Small steps like this build the case that lifespan is set by concrete, testable pathways.
plos-pone-0002252:
Iñigo Angulo-Barturen, María Belén Jiménez-Díaz, Teresa Mulet, and co-authors built a mouse model for the deadliest malaria parasite, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum causes most malaria deaths, and new drugs and vaccines are urgently needed. Testing them was blocked by a simple fact: the parasite infects human red blood cells almost exclusively, so standard lab animals would not do.

The team engrafted mice with human red blood cells and selected parasite strains able to grow in them. The resulting model lets researchers test drugs against falciparum malaria in a living system. A reliable animal model speeds every step of antimalarial drug development.
plos-pone-0002352:
Igor Petrunia and co-authors checked a safety question in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Could a plant bacterium that entered mouse blood switch on genes in mouse organs? Agrobacterium tumefaciens is the main tool for moving genes into plants, and its host range can stretch to other organisms in the lab. Agrobacterium species have also been isolated from human bloodstream infections.

That raised a safety question: could bacteraemia, bacteria in the blood, lead the bacterium to deliver its genes into animal tissues? The team reports it did not lead to reporter gene expression in mouse organs. The negative result is reassuring for the medical safety of a workhorse of plant biotechnology.
plos-pone-0002452:
Led by Hunter, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Melissa G. Hunter, Morgan McLemore, Daniel C. Link, and others. Its subject is divergent Pathways in COS-7 Cells Mediate Defective Internalization and Intracellular Routing of Truncated G-CSFR Forms in SCN/AML. Expression of truncated G-CSFR forms in patients with SCN/AML induces hyperproliferation and prolonged cell survival.

before, we showed that ligand internalization is delayed and degradation of truncated G-CSFR forms is defective in patients with SCN/AML. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002552:
Research by Silva and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Nathan Silva, William C. Smith, and others. Its subject is inverse Correlation of Population Similarity and Introduction Date for Invasive Ascidians. The genomes of many marine invertebrates, including the purple sea urchin and the solitary ascidians Ciona intestinalis and Ciona savignyi.

Analysis of the C. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002652:
Work by Yujun Cui and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was insight into microevolution of yersinia pestis by clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Yujun Cui, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Yersinia pestis , the pathogen of plague, has greatly influenced human history on a global scale. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002752:
Work by Berta Victoria and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was conservation of the s10-spc-α locus within otherwise highly plastic genomes provides phylogenetic insight into the genus leptospira. The catalog record names Berta Victoria first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. S10-spc-α is a 17.5 kb cluster of 32 genes encoding ribosomal proteins. The authors add a further point. This locus has an unusual composition and organization in Leptospira interrogans . For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002852:
Work by Nikola Sprigg and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a randomised controlled trial of triple antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin, clopidogrel and dipyridamole) in the secondary prevention of stroke: safety, tolerability and feasibility. Authorship is credited in the record to Nikola Sprigg and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Aspirin, dipyridamole and clopidogrel are effective in secondary vascular prevention. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002952:
Amanda Antons, Rui Wang, Spyros Kalams and co-authors measured how signal strength changes suppression by regulatory T cells in 2008. Regulatory T cells, or Tregs, calm immune responses to self and foreign targets alike. They need activation through their receptor and the signal IL-2 before they can suppress.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team varied how strongly T cells were activated and watched Treg suppression of HIV-specific and general responses. Suppression depended on signal strength, as the title says. The detail matters for HIV, where both weak defense and excess activation cause harm. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003052:
Stephen Smith, David Tank, Lori-Ann Boulanger and co-authors argued in 2008 for stronger protection of endophytes. A key case for conserving biodiversity is that undiscovered species will yield products of great use to humans. That link was largely conjectural when the paper was written.

Endophytes are microbes living inside plants. Using direct bioassay evidence, the team supports the claim that such hidden life can yield bioactive compounds. Their title says bioactive endophytes warrant intensified exploration and conservation. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper ties drug discovery to habitat protection with data rather than hope.
plos-pone-0003152:
Ruud M. Buijs, Jan van der Vliet, Mari-Laure Garidou and colleagues trace how the brain talks to the spleen in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Vagus nerve output from the central nervous system had lately been shown to suppress the innate immune defence against pathogens. The team used anatomy and physiology methods to study brain-spleen communication directly.

The title gives the result: cutting the vagus supply to the spleen stopped the making of antibodies against antigens in the blood. Readers see hard evidence that nerves help set antibody output. The work links brain circuits to immune control in a concrete way.
plos-pone-0003252:
Torsten Thomas and co-authors read the genome of a sea bacterium in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In the sea, germs crowd onto host surfaces like seaweed and shell-less animals, where they compete hard with each other. Pseudoalteromonas tunicata is a winner on such surfaces, known for holding its ground against rivals.

Their genome scan shows traits of a life lived stuck to surfaces in the sea. Readers see genes matched to that attached life style. Such traits, from glues to germ-killing tools, interest work on ship fouling and on new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0003352:
Helene A. Haeberle, Carin Dürrstein, Peter Rosenberger and colleagues study a hypoxia factor during viral infection in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha is a transcription factor that functions as master regulator of mammalian oxygen homeostasis. Recent studies also identified a role for HIF-1 alpha as transcriptional regulator during inflammation or infection.

The title reports oxygen-independent stabilization of HIF-1 during RSV infection. Readers learn a respiratory virus can switch on an oxygen sensor without low oxygen. That crosstalk may worsen airway inflammation, and it suggests HIF blockers could be tested in severe viral infection.
plos-pone-0003452:
Marina Cardó-Vila and co-authors pulled a drug clue from a cancer patient in this 2008 paper. They screened fragments selected in that patient for useful binders. One peptide matched part of human interleukin-11, a signaling protein. Interleukin-11 is already approved to treat low platelet counts after chemotherapy.

The peptide mapped to domain I of the protein. That spot is where the protein meets its receptor. A binder for that site could tune the signal up or down. The work gives drug designers a foothold on a cancer-related pathway. Screens drawn from patients can surface binders that pure lab design might miss.
plos-pone-0003552:
Meredith E. Young, Geoffrey R. Norman, and Karin R. Humphreys studied media effects on disease fear in this 2008 paper. Global talk of pandemics has raised reporting on outbreaks. Heavy coverage may shift how risky diseases seem to the public. Their studies tested that influence directly.

High levels of press reporting changed perceptions of disease. Readers judged covered diseases as more threatening than facts warranted. The popular press thus sets the public sense of danger. Health officials must plan messages with that power in mind. Outbreak scares show this effect at its strongest in daily news cycles.
plos-pone-0003652:
Reuben Saba, Chelsey D. Goodman, Rhiannon L. C. H. Huzarewich, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces that tune how genes are used in cells. Little was known about their part in diseases where brain tissue breaks down.

The team profiled microRNAs in prion disease, where misfolded proteins damage the brain. A set pattern of changes appeared as the disease advanced, forming a signature of the damage. Such a signature could help track the disease and point to steps where failing neurons might be helped.
plos-pone-0003752:
Francisco Caiado, Carla Real, Tânia Carvalho, and colleagues published this vascular study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cells from bone marrow can become vascular precursor cells that help build new blood vessels. They take part in normal vessel growth, cancer growth, low blood flow repair, and wound healing.

The team adjusted Notch signaling in these precursor cells. Tuning that pathway changed the cells' power to grow vessels and support healing. The dial offers a way to control the body's own repair crew, for better vessel growth where tissue needs it.
plos-pone-0003852:
Antje Fischer-Rosinsky, Eva Fisher, Peter Kovacs, and colleagues published this meta-analysis in PLOS ONE in 2008. SOCS3 links cytokine signals to insulin resistance, making it a candidate gene for type 2 diabetes. A common variant, A+930 to G, had been picked from HapMap data as the tag to test.

The authors pooled four independent study populations to test that variant. They found no association between the SOCS3 tagging variant and type 2 diabetes. The clear negative result closes the case on one suspect and lets diabetes genetics focus its search elsewhere.
plos-pone-0003952:
Sara K. Lindén, Timothy H. J. Florin, and Michael A. McGuckin reviewed mucus changes during gut infection in 2008. Bacterial gut infections sicken and kill people around the world. A mouse infection with Citrobacter rodentium models two human E. coli diseases. Mucus glycoproteins form the gut's first protective layer.

Their PLOS ONE article follows how that mucus layer changes during infection. The mucins shift in amount and type as bacteria attack. Those shifts can help or hinder the germs that live there. Knowing the pattern clarifies how the gut defends its lining. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004052:
Jeffrey W. Habig, P. Joseph Aruscavage, and Brenda L. Bass studied gene silencing in worms in 2008. RNA interference starts when Dicer cuts double-stranded RNA into small pieces. In C. elegans, Dicer needs a helper protein called RDE-4. Without it, RNA interference normally fails at step one.

Their PLOS ONE article reports high RNA doses bypass that need. With enough trigger RNA, silencing worked even without RDE-4. The exception reveals a backup route into the silencing machinery. Dose effects like this matter for labs designing RNA experiments. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004152:
Anirban Chakraborty and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and their building blocks, ribosomal proteins, do more than hold the factory together. One of them, L11, was recently shown to control the tumour suppressor p53 by binding its regulator MDM2.

Using zebrafish embryos, the team asked what happens to development when L11 is lost. They report that losing L11 disrupts embryonic development through a cell-death response that depends on p53. The finding links a ribosome part to the guard system that decides whether damaged cells live or die.
plos-pone-0004252:
Andrew Farke, Ewan Wolff, and Darren Tanke published this dinosaur study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The horns and frill of Triceratops have been read two ways: as display structures or as weapons used against rivals and predators. Lesions in the bone, including reactive bone growth, healing fractures, and possible punctures, offer a way to test the weapon idea.

The authors gathered evidence of such injuries on Triceratops skulls. They present it as evidence of combat between these dinosaurs. If the marks match fighting, the great frill was not just a billboard but a shield in real fights.
plos-pone-0004352:
John Hagan and colleagues published this imprinting study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genomic imprinting is an exception to Mendelian genetics: imprinted genes are expressed from only one parent's copy, depending on parental origin. In mammals these genes are critical in development and physiology, and faulty imprinting is tied to disease.

The team defined the imprinted Dlk1-Dio3 cluster on mouse chromosome 12qF1. They report that at least ten genes define the cluster. The cluster sits on mouse chromosome 12, in the band called qF1. A full census of the region is the groundwork for understanding the disorders tied to it.
plos-pone-0004452:
Sounds in sloppy speech blur into their neighbors, and Kambiz Tavabi, Ludger Elling, Christian Dobel, and co-authors watched the brain handle that blur in PLOS ONE in 2009. In casual talk, a sound often takes on traits of the sounds beside it. A key trait is place of articulation, where in the mouth the sound is made.

Using a method that records the brain's magnetic fields, the team tracked nerve activity while listeners heard sounds whose place had shifted. They asked how the auditory system sorts a changed sound back to the right one. The work shows the brain does not just hear raw sound; it repairs it. That repair is part of why people understand fast, careless speech with so little effort.
plos-pone-0004552:
Marks added to a protein called Bicaudal-D are sorted one by one by Rafael Koch, Romana Ledermann, Olivier Urwyler, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Phosphorylation, the adding of phosphate marks, controls almost all processes in biology after proteins are made. Mass spectrometry had recently found many new mark sites across whole proteomes, but the function of most sites was unknown.

The team studied the serine phosphorylation sites of Bicaudal-D, a protein needed for development in flies. One mutant form leaves females sterile. Their systematic analysis, including intragenic suppression, where a second change cancels a first, shows which marks matter. Work like this turns long lists of chemical marks into actual understanding of protein control.
plos-pone-0004652:
Signals inside white blood cells set how fast they crawl through tissue, show Daniel Graham, Bernd Zinselmeyer, Francesca Mascarenhas, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. In response to infection, neutrophils are quickly recruited from the blood into inflamed tissues. Their migration between cells is crucial for capturing and controlling fast-growing microbes before microbial growth overwhelms the host's defenses.

The signals run through ITAM motifs and the Vav family of exchange factors, proteins that switch on other proteins. The team shows this signaling regulates the interstitial transit rates of neutrophils in living animals. In plain terms, the same machinery that arms a neutrophil also sets its speed. Tuning that speed could help in diseases of too much or too little inflammation.
plos-pone-0004752:
Ritwij Kulkarni and colleagues tested two secretion systems as drivers of kidney infecting E. coli virulence, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many gut bacteria use these systems to inject or shed factors that help them infect. Their kinship suggests shared roots, yet their roles in gut external E. coli strains were not yet determined.

The team knocked out parts of each system and tested infection strength. Knowing which systems truly drive kidney infection focuses drug and vaccine work. It also helps sort harmless gut strains from those that invade the urinary tract. Such traits guide diagnosis too. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004852:
Anthony Papadopoulos made a hydrodynamics based case for the power law polynomial function in animal swimming energetics, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The first degree power law polynomial is frequently used to describe activity metabolism for steady swimming animals. The function evaluates key energetic cost parameters such as standard metabolic rate in hydrodynamics based metabolic studies across fish and other aquatic species.

Papadopoulos argues the form fits physical principles well. Proper working forms prevent biased cost estimates. Swimming energetics informs ecology and aquaculture. Theory and measurement should align. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004952:
In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks myelin. Myelin is the insulation around nerve fibers. Enzymes called matrix metalloproteinases help chop up myelin basic protein. Sergey Shiryaev and co-authors studied that chopping in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked whether the fragments provoke the immune attack.

The team examined how the enzymes cut the main forms of myelin basic protein. They identified the immunogenic peptides that result. Those fragments are targets the misguided immune response recognizes. Naming them exactly matters for therapy design. Drug designers gain precise pieces to block in autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0005052:
Lung adenocarcinoma is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide. It kills mostly because it spreads early. Chang-Han Chen and colleagues traced one spread mechanism in PLOS ONE in 2009. The vessel-growth signal VEGFA was their starting point. They found it switches up a gene called FLJ10540.

The raised FLJ10540 helps lung cancer cells migrate and invade. The effect runs through the PI3K/AKT pathway. That chain reveals a new route for metastasis. Blocking it could slow lung cancer's march. The study connects a famous growth factor to an obscure gene. Obscure genes can hold the keys to spread. Naming the chain gives drug hunters a target list.
plos-pone-0005152:
Gene researchers compare genomes to test ideas. They often pick DNA regions where species differ greatly. That cherry-picking skews later statistics. Andrew Kern derived a correction for the problem in PLOS ONE in 2009. The skewed statistic is the site frequency spectrum. It sums up the genetic variation in a sample.

Choosing regions by divergence biases the spectrum. His correction restores honest comparisons. The fix cleans up a core genetics tool. Genome comparison drives new ideas in the field. Biased inputs quietly poison those ideas. A sound correction protects many future studies. The work is technical but basic to the field. It makes species comparisons mean what researchers think they mean.
plos-pone-0005252:
What a predator eats can be read from DNA left in its gut or droppings. Older tests needed a guess at the menu first, or a custom design for each case. Dunshea presented a general DNA-based diet method in PLOS ONE in 2009 that needs no prior diet knowledge.

A universal approach can detect diverse prey in samples from any predator. That frees diet studies from guesswork and one-off assays. Ecologists can use it to map food webs, track endangered predators, and check what invasive species are eating. Park staff and farmers could use the same test to learn what foxes, cats, or rats eat, with no need to watch them hunt at night.
plos-pone-0005352:
West Nile virus has spread worldwide and become an important pathogen for people and domestic animals. Koo and colleagues mapped how its proteins have changed over the virus's known history in PLOS ONE in 2009, sorting conserved parts from variable ones.

Sites that stay conserved across many strains are often essential to the virus. Those stable sites are the best targets for vaccines and drugs, since the virus cannot easily change them. The map also shows which regions vary freely and would make poor targets. Birds and horses also catch this virus from mosquito bites, so the stable core map helps vets guard stock and warns health teams where the virus may spread next year.
plos-pone-0005452:
Lori Albergotti and co-authors studied membranes that surround growing embryos, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. All land vertebrates form these membranes, which move gases and water, clear waste, and cushion the embryo. In animals that give birth to live young, the membranes also pass food from the mother.

The team tested whether the membranes make hormones, a job long linked mainly with the placenta. They found signs of hormone activity in membranes of animals without a placenta too. That widens the picture of how embryos are supported and how live birth may have evolved.
plos-pone-0005552:
Anna Grimsrud and co-authors studied blood pressure and mental health in South Africa in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Growing evidence links high blood pressure with depression and anxiety in rich countries. Far less was known about that link in poorer countries.

Using a survey that covered the whole country, the team compared adults with high blood pressure against others. They checked how often depression and anxiety appeared in each group. Local evidence like this helps clinics in South Africa plan care that treats body and mind together. Findings from one national sample cannot be stretched to other countries without local checks of their own.
plos-pone-0005652:
Melissa Rotunno and co-authors studied metabolic genes and lung cancer risk in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Some enzymes switch on the cancer-causing chemicals in tobacco smoke. Gene variants that change those enzymes could explain why only some smokers develop lung cancer.

Past studies were small and measured smoke exposure poorly. The team tested many variants at once and also measured gene activity in lung tissue. Combining the two gives a firmer view of which metabolic genes truly move lung cancer risk. Larger samples with careful exposure records are what earlier work lacked, and this study was built to supply both.
plos-pone-0005752:
Harpinder Randhawa and co-authors sped up the breeding of improved wheat in 2009 using DNA markers. Breeders often need to move one good gene into a popular wheat variety without dragging in unwanted traits. The usual fix, repeated backcrossing, takes many seasons.

Their marker-assisted method checks seedlings for the target gene and for the share of the parent genome restored. With it, over ninety-seven percent of the parent genome returns in just two backcross rounds. That speed lets breeders add disease resistance or quality traits to trusted varieties fast. The four-step method is spelled out for other programs to copy.
plos-pone-0005852:
Silvia Wognum and co-authors traced in 2009 how spinal cord injury remodels the bladder wall over time. Injury to the cord often leaves the bladder inflamed, scarred, and prone to infection. Those changes build through many pathways at once.

The team ran an exploratory pathways analysis on rat bladder tissue after injury. Patterns of gene activity pointed to linked waves of remodeling and inflammation. Seeing the sequence helps decide when each kind of treatment might work best. The study is an early map for a complication that weighs heavily on life after spinal injury.
plos-pone-0005952:
How a person looks at a face may say something about who they are. Susan Perlman, James Morris, Brent Vander Wyk and colleagues tested that idea in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They focused on traits like neuroticism, a tendency toward worry and low mood, and tracked where people's eyes went as they viewed faces.

Gaze patterns differed by trait, the team reports, so the eyes follow character as well as the scene. That link helps explain why social life feels so different from one person to the next. The study also gives feeling and social behavior research a simple, hard measure: where the eyes rest, and for how long.
plos-pone-0006052:
Short stretches of protein, called linear motifs, are the handshakes by which proteins find each other. Claudia Chica, Francesca Diella and Toby Gibson asked in 2009 how those handshakes evolve. Their PLOS ONE paper tests whether a motif changes over time together with the regions that flank it, since a motif's job depends heavily on its setting.

Evidence favors concerted evolution, the title reports: motif and flanks change as a unit. Functional motifs mostly sit in loose, flexible parts of proteins, where context is everything. The result guides how scientists read protein sequences, since a motif lifted out of its neighborhood may tell only half its story.
plos-pone-0006152:
One human protein touches viral switches, a growth pathway and the machinery that extends gene messages. Ella Reiss-Sklan, Alexander Levitzki and Tally Naveh-Many studied how that protein's own levels are set in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper examines the complex regulation of HIC, the human I-mfa domain containing protein, which differentially regulates transcription from viral promoters.

HIC affects the Wnt pathway, the JNK pathway and a factor that elongates messages, so its control is a hub of hubs. Mapping how HIC expression is governed explains when this multitasker rises and falls. The work serves both virology and signaling research, which meet in this one unusually connected protein.
plos-pone-0006252:
Female mammals switch off one of their two X chromosomes so gene doses match males. Michael Cantrell, Bryan Carstens, and Holly Wichman studied that silencing in a rodent lacking LINE-1 activity, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The silencer is Xist, a large RNA that coats the chromosome from its control centre.

LINE-1 elements, jumping DNA pieces scattered over the X, were thought to help the coating spread. Yet X inactivation and Xist evolution proceeded in this rodent without them. The result loosens a long-held part of the standard model. It shows the silencing system is more flexible than assumed.
plos-pone-0006352:
A malaria vaccine could stop the parasite in mosquitoes instead of in people. Debabani Roy Chowdhury and colleagues built such a transmission-blocking vaccine in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. It targets Pfs48/45, a protein on the sexual stage of Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite.

The full-length protein was produced in E. coli bacteria using codon harmonisation, matching the gene's rhythm to the host. Cheap bacterial production matters for a vaccine aimed at poor regions. Malaria killed nearly a million people a year at the time. Blocking transmission protects whole communities, not just the vaccinated.
plos-pone-0006452:
Oliver Pergams and Joshua Lawler documented fast body change in rodents in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapid change in mammal shape has rarely been recorded. Known cases were almost all rodents on islands. There, change is usually blamed on release from rivals or on founder effects, where a few starters set the traits of a new group.

The authors report that recent, widespread change goes well beyond islands. Rodents in many places have shifted shape in a short time. That breadth hints at broad drivers, such as climate or human land use. The study turns rare island stories into a general pattern worth explaining.
plos-pone-0006552:
Meng Zhao and co-authors studied how a leukemia-linked protein is destroyed in PLOS ONE in 2009. Healthy tissue keeps a tight balance between cell growth, cell change, and cell death. A family of proteins called C/EBP helps hold that balance. The team studied one member, C/EBP alpha, in leukemia cells pushed toward death.

Their title says an enzyme called protein kinase C delta drives the shredding of C/EBP alpha as the death program starts. The shredder is the proteasome, the cell's own protein disposal unit. How this factor is lost shapes whether cells die or mature. The work may inform leukemia care that forces cells to grow up or die.
plos-pone-0006652:
Neha Agrawal, Nisha Padmanabhan, and Gaiti Hasan studied a calcium channel in fly insulin cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. The inositol trisphosphate receptor is an intracellular ligand-gated channel. It releases calcium from intracellular stores in response to extracellular signals. The team examined its function in Drosophila insulin producing cells.

Insulin cells in flies parallel pancreatic beta cells in humans. Calcium signals control insulin release in both. A receptor that gates calcium therefore shapes metabolism and growth. Fly genetics allow precise tests of its role in living animals. The work connects a universal channel to hormone control.
plos-pone-0006752:
Carmen H. Coxon and colleagues tested whether a cell division driver could restart growth in heart cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adult heart muscle cells have left the cell cycle. After birth they stop dividing and fully mature. That is why heart damage, such as a heart attack, cannot be repaired by regrowth. The protein Plk1 helps drive division in other cells.

The team overexpressed Plk1 in rat cardiac myocytes in culture. Despite the extra protein, the cells did not divide. The negative result is itself useful knowledge. It shows one division switch is not enough for heart cells. Heart repair strategies will likely need different or combined levers.
plos-pone-0006852:
Hiroshi Nishiura, Don Klinkenberg, and Mick Roberts tackled early severity estimates for emerging diseases in PLOS ONE in 2009. The case fatality ratio measures a disease's virulence. It divides deaths by total cases. During a running epidemic, that simple ratio is biased. Deaths lag behind cases, distorting the picture.

The authors used an influenza pandemic as a case study. They assessed how to estimate virulence early and honestly. Early estimates steer hospital planning and public messaging. A biased low figure invites complacency, while a high one invites panic. Their methods aim to give officials a defensible early number.
plos-pone-0006952:
Alexandra Magold, Matthias Cacquevel, and Patrick Fraering profiled gene activity in altered cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. They worked with cells whose gamma-secretase activity was enhanced. Gamma-secretase cuts many membrane proteins inside cells. The cut frees inner fragments that travel to the nucleus and switch genes on or off.

The authors measured which genes changed when this cutting ran high. Those shifts reveal the reach of gamma-secretase signaling. The enzyme is famous for its role in amyloid production in Alzheimer's disease. Mapping its full gene program helps separate its normal jobs from its harmful ones.
plos-pone-0007052:
Fabio Arnesano, Simone Scintilla, Vincenza Calò, and colleagues studied metal effects on a cleanup protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. Brain disorders such as Parkinson's share common features. Proteins misfold and clump, the disposal system fails, and metal levels rise in the brain. The clumps often contain ubiquitin, the tag protein of that disposal system.

The team tested what copper does to ubiquitin itself. Copper triggered ubiquitin to aggregate. That is a striking twist, since the tag protein should prevent clumping. It suggests metals may sabotage the cleanup machinery directly, worsening the protein jams of these diseases.
plos-pone-0007152:
Fu-Shi Quan, Yeu-Chun Kim, Dae-Goon Yoo, and colleagues tested a flu vaccine patch in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flu shots are advised every year, so easy delivery matters. A patch carrying vaccine-coated microneedles could give vaccine through the skin. The team reasoned this route might improve protection over a standard shot.

They stabilized the vaccine for coating onto microneedles. Mice given the patch were protected better than controls. Skin is rich in immune cells, which may explain the gain. A patch that ships without needles or nurses could transform flu campaigns.
plos-pone-0007252:
Alex Mesoudi examined the cultural dynamics of copycat suicide in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Suicides sometimes cluster in space or time. Such clusters led researchers to suggest social learning, where exposure to one suicide raises the chance of others nearby, a pattern called copycat suicide.

Mesoudi analyzes point clusters, groups of suicides localized in both time and space. He studies how cultural transmission could produce those clusters. His work treats suicide contagion as a testable social process rather than a simple assumption. The analysis informs prevention work that watches media coverage and local clusters carefully.
plos-pone-0007352:
Verena Olivier, Jessica Queen, and Karla J. F. Satchell worked out how cholera bacteria colonize mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Vibrio cholerae colonizes the small intestine of adult mice of a common lab strain. The physical and genetic conditions that allow that colonization were investigated in this study.

The authors report successful colonization requires ketamine anesthesia. It also requires accessory toxins produced by the bacterium. Neutralizing stomach acid was part of the successful protocol. Their PLOS ONE recipe gives researchers a workable adult mouse model of cholera, which is valuable for testing vaccines and treatments.
plos-pone-0007452:
Oscar Pich and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Mycoplasma genitalium, one of the smallest known bacteria. The cell carries a single structure called the terminal organelle. It serves adhesion, movement, and division. Before the cell divides, that structure must be duplicated in a coordinated way. The team asked what keeps duplication under control.

They found that two proteins, P110 and P140, act as negative effectors of the process. In plain terms, these proteins hold duplication back until the right moment. Such restraint matters in a cell with very little spare machinery. The work shows that even a minimal bacterium runs tight scheduling on its parts. That precision is part of how the tiny organism stays viable.
plos-pone-0007552:
Muhammad Tariq and colleagues published a clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on treating cholera, the infection famous for sudden, watery diarrhea. The fluid loss can drain the body so fast that the kidneys fail. The team studied how dehydrated patients were on arrival. They also recorded the fluid volumes needed to treat them and the blood values marking kidney stress.

Patients required massive amounts of fluid to recover. The researchers also flagged an unusual ratio between two blood markers, BUN and creatinine, in early kidney failure. That ratio may help clinicians spot pre-renal failure sooner in cholera cases. Concrete numbers matter in outbreaks, where staff treat many patients fast. The study gives them measured guidance for one of the world's most dehydrating diseases.
plos-pone-0007652:
Annalisa Grimaldi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on muscle regeneration in the leech. In vertebrates, certain cells carry markers of both muscle and blood vessel lineage. Those myoendothelial cells can become muscle and help repair it. Many questions about them remain open. Leeches regenerate muscle robustly, making them a simple place to study the cells. The team set out to find, isolate, and grow the leech version.

They identified myoendothelial cells in leech tissue and expanded them in culture. Cells with dual identity survived the move to the dish. That gives researchers a workable model of a cell type that is rare and hard to study in mammals. Regeneration biology needs such simple windows. The leech, an old medical animal, becomes a modern laboratory for muscle repair.
plos-pone-0007752:
Cameron Brennan and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It seeks a better way to sort glioblastoma, a lethal brain cancer. The name glioblastoma multiforme covers a mixed group of tumors. Past schemes sorted them by how they behaved or which cells they resembled.

This team sorted tumors by the activity of their signaling pathways. They paired that with the tumors' genetic changes. Distinct subclasses emerged from the combined view. Sorting cancers by active pathways can point to drugs that block those pathways. It is a step toward treatment matched to each tumor.
plos-pone-0007852:
Richard Bomphrey and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures how blowflies fly in normal, everyday flight. Insects are famous for bursts of extreme performance. Yet little was known about their routine flight, the normal envelope they use most of the time.

The team built a novel arena with corner-cube reflectors to track free flight. They benchmarked the flight of the blowfly Calliphora vicina. Their method records speed, turns and climbs during ordinary behavior. Engineers designing tiny flying robots need exactly this kind of data. Nature's routine is a better template than its emergencies.
plos-pone-0007952:
Stephane Doly and colleagues traced the pull of the drug MDMA in mouse brains for PLOS ONE in 2009. MDMA, also called ecstasy, floods the brain with serotonin and dopamine by reversing their transport pumps. The team focused on one serotonin receptor, the 5-HT2B type.

Mice work showed this receptor plays a real part in the drug's rewarding pull. Block or remove that part, and the drug's hold on behavior weakens. Naming the receptor gives addiction research a clear target and helps explain why the drug feels so strong to users.
plos-pone-0008052:
Henry Zot and colleagues offered a new account of how muscle holds steady force in PLOS ONE in 2009. Muscle contracts when calcium frees a blocking strand so fibers can grip and pull. The classic model of that balance was the Hill model, long used alone.

Their account treats the muscle as resting among several balanced states at once. That picture fits both the grip data and the S-shaped force curve that the classic model strains to match. A truer model of the grip helps all work built on it, from heart studies to prosthetic design.
plos-pone-0008152:
Amanda-Jayne Carr and colleagues grafted lab-grown eye cells into rats losing their sight in PLOS ONE in 2009. The graft cells were retinal pigment cells, the support layer for the eye's light sensors, grown from human iPS cells. In many blinding diseases that support layer fails first.

Placed in the eyes of retinal dystrophy rats, the grafts lived and slowed the loss of the rats' own light sensors. Protection, not just survival of the graft, is the result that matters. It moves stem-cell eye care from a hope toward a testable treatment.
plos-pone-0008252:
Craig D. H. Sherman, Erik Wapstra, and Mats Olsson studied fatherhood patterns in frogs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many studies use paternity success as a stand-in for fertilization success. That shortcut can mislead when embryos die at different rates. In Peron's tree frog, females may mate with several males. Sperm competition then shapes which males father offspring.

The authors tracked paternity skew across development, from embryo to later stages. A consistent skew through ontogeny suggests the pattern is set early. Their check validates paternity as a measure in this species. It also warns researchers to test that assumption elsewhere.
plos-pone-0008352:
Ram Naresh, Yong Song, and David J. Hampson studied a gut spirochete in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Brachyspira pilosicoli is an anaerobic spiral bacterium that received little study. It grows slowly and needs specialized culture conditions. The bacterium colonizes the large intestine of many species, including humans. Typically it forms a dense layer attached to the gut surface.

The team watched it attach to cultured Caco-2 cells, a human gut cell line. Attachment induced pathological changes in those cells. Such changes help explain symptoms of intestinal spirochete infection. The work uses cell culture to model colonization.
plos-pone-0008452:
Rashid Uz Zaman and co-authors tracked flu in Bangladesh in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Past work in a poor part of Dhaka found flu was common in children. The team set up hospital checks across the whole country. They watched patients who came to clinics with flu-like illness. Cases covered all age groups in the years 2007 and 2008.

Their data show how flu spreads and when it peaks in Bangladesh. They note which groups are hit most and in which months. Such facts help plan vaccine timing and hospital load. The study gives a national picture where only local data existed before.
plos-pone-0008552:
Julie Pendergast and co-authors split the roles of two clock genes in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The mouse circadian system sets daily rhythms in behavior and body function. A master pacemaker sits in the brain's suprachiasmatic nuclei. Other oscillators run in brain and body tissues. Lesions of the master pacemaker abolish daily rhythms. The genes Period2 and Period3 are core clock parts, but their distinct jobs were unclear.

Using in vitro analysis of cells and tissues, the team separate their functions. Each gene contributes in a different way to rhythm strength and timing. That split helps explain how the clock stays robust. It refines models of the mammalian timekeeping system.
plos-pone-0008652:
Elizabeth Hemond and co-authors study a threatened coral in Florida in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Staghorn coral, Acropora cervicornis, once dominated shallow Caribbean waters. Over three decades, white-band disease devastated its populations. Both staghorn and elkhorn corals are now listed as threatened under US law. The team measure genetic diversity and connectivity in Florida staghorn populations. Connectivity shows how larvae move between reefs.

They find Florida populations retain diversity but show structured connectivity. Some reefs exchange larvae freely, others are more isolated. Restoration should source corals with that structure in mind. Genetic data can guide where to plant nursery corals for best survival.
plos-pone-0008752:
Assaf Zohar, Noa Dekel, Boris Rubinsky, and colleagues proposed a new way voltage moves charge in receptors. Their study, mixing theory with experiments, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. GPCRs are docking proteins that relay many drug and hormone signals. Recent work found small currents when membrane voltage changes near them. Those currents also shift how strongly a signal molecule binds.

The authors modeled where the moving charge might sit. Experiments then checked the model's predictions. A voltage-sensitive step inside the receptor could explain both findings. The idea widens how scientists think about receptors long treated as voltage-blind.
plos-pone-0008852:
Jamila Khallou-Laschet, Aditi Varthaman, Giulia Fornasa, and colleagues asked how flexible artery macrophages can be. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Macrophages drive atherosclerosis, the artery clogging behind heart attacks. They can take inflammatory or healing stances. Mice lacking apolipoprotein E develop the disease reliably. The team tracked macrophage stances as plaques progressed.

Cells shifted their stance as disease stages changed. That plasticity means a macrophage is not fixed as friend or foe. Therapies might push them toward healing stances at the right moment. Timing such pushes becomes a design question for heart drugs.
plos-pone-0008952:
Luc Tremblay and Thanh Nguyen tested how a sight-and-sound trick changes while a person reaches, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The brain merges what the eyes see and the ears hear into one picture of the world. Vision usually wins when the two senses disagree, creating illusions. The pair asked whether acting on a goal changes that balance in the moment.

Volunteers reached toward targets while the researchers played the audio-visual illusion. During the reach itself, people were less fooled than when sitting still. Sensitivity to the trick dropped in real time, as the movement unfolded. The result suggests the brain tunes its senses differently when guiding an action.
plos-pone-0009052:
Lan Chen and co-authors watched a Parkinson's-linked protein melt under sugar attack, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Alpha-synuclein is the main building block of Lewy bodies, the clumps found in Parkinson's brains. Sugars can stick to proteins in a process called glycation, warping their shape. Glucose-driven damage to alpha-synuclein had been studied before.

Ribose, another sugar, warped the protein much faster. It folded into molten globules classed as advanced glycation end products. These blobs proved highly toxic to cells. A fast sugar route to toxic synuclein may matter in diabetes-linked brain disease.
plos-pone-0009152:
Geqiang Li and co-authors showed two signals teaming up to keep blood stem cells young, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gab adaptor proteins relay signals from cytokine receptors in blood cells. Gab2 tunes two major pathways that govern cell growth and survival. Hematopoietic stem cells must maintain themselves for a lifetime of blood making.

Gab2 worked synergistically with STAT5, a signal carrier in those cells. Together they promoted stem cell maintenance and self-renewal. Each alone did less than the pair working in concert. Knowing the partnership may improve growing blood stem cells for transplants.
plos-pone-0009252:
Julian Maggini and co-authors published this immune therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mesenchymal stromal cells, taken from bone marrow, are prized in medicine. Part of their power is that they can calm the immune system. That calming effect matters as much as their ability to become other cell types.

The team placed these stromal cells with macrophages, immune cells that drive inflammation. The stromal cells turned the activated macrophages toward a regulatory-like profile. In that state, macrophages soothe rather than attack. The finding helps explain how stromal cell therapy might quiet diseases driven by overactive immunity.
plos-pone-0009352:
Guang Guo and co-authors published this behavior genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A gene called DAT1 controls the dopamine transporter, which clears dopamine from synapses. Versions of the gene differ in a repeated stretch of DNA. The authors tested one specific claim about the 9R/9R version.

They proposed that 9R/9R protects against a wide range of risky behaviors. Using data measured three times, they compared it with the other common versions. They also factored in whether each behavior was legal or not. The study tests whether a single gene variant can tilt many choices at once, from habits to rule-breaking.
plos-pone-0009452:
Andreas Zautner and co-authors looked for the cause of repeat tonsillitis in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many patients get sore, infected tonsils again and again. Drugs often fail, and surgery is used only after many failed courses. The team searched tonsil tissue for germs that could explain the returns.

They found Staphylococcus aureus living inside tonsil cells in many cases. Hidden inside cells, the germ is shielded from drugs that work in open tissue. That hiding place helps explain why the illness keeps coming back. Care that can reach germs inside cells may cut the need for surgery.
plos-pone-0009552:
Abdul Wakeel, Xiaofeng Zhang, and Jere McBride examined proteins of a tick borne germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ehrlichia chaffeensis infects people through tick bites. It makes a small set of proteins built from repeated blocks. Those proteins run oddly heavy on lab gels. Sugar tags were long blamed for the extra size. The team used mass spectrometry to read the proteins directly.

Their readings showed phosphate tags on the proteins instead. They found no sign of the sugar tags once assumed. Correcting the record matters for vaccine design. A vaccine must match the germ's proteins as they truly are, tags included.
plos-pone-0009652:
Ayako Chino, Kenji Watanabe, and Hisao Moriya built plasmids inside yeast in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plasmids are small circles of DNA that carry genes into cells for study. Building them is daily work in genetics labs. Fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe, is skilled at recombining DNA, stitching matching pieces together. The team used that skill to assemble plasmids within the yeast itself.

DNA pieces fed to the yeast were joined into complete plasmids by its own machinery. The method skips several fussy steps of test tube assembly. It turns a humble fungus into a living workshop for gene construction. Labs that work with this yeast gain a simpler route to custom DNA.
plos-pone-0009852:
Therapeutic vaccines aim to train the immune system of people already infected with HIV. Bernard Macatangay and colleagues studied what holds that training back. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The patients were on ART, antiretroviral therapy that controls the virus.

Regulatory T cells are immune cells whose job is to calm other immune cells. After vaccination, they suppressed the Gag-specific CD8 response the vaccine tried to build. Polyfunctional responses, where one cell does several jobs, are prized in vaccine design. The result flags a brake that future vaccines must work around.
plos-pone-0009952:
Tularemia bacteria are dangerous enough that testing vaccines needs a faithful animal model. Heather Ray and colleagues showed a common lab rat fits that role. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Francisella causes tularemia, also called rabbit fever.

The rat is the Fischer 344 strain, long used in research. It reflects human susceptibility to Francisella pulmonary challenge, infection through the lungs. That match makes it a new platform for studying virulence and protection. A good model speeds the search for vaccines and treatments. Rat models are cheaper and hardier than many alternatives.
plos-pone-0010152:
The authors were Huan Nguyen, Terrence Tumpey, Hae-Jung Park, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested bird antibodies against flu in mice. Pandemic flu threatens world health and economies, and vaccines take time to develop. Giving ready-made antibodies, called passive immunization, offers another route to prevent or treat infection.

The team made antibodies in birds against two flu strains, H5N1 and H1N1. They tested those antibodies both before exposure and as treatment. Protection in mice would support antibody stockpiles as a stopgap while strain-matched vaccines are prepared. The paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010252:
The authors were Yen-Hoon Luah, Balbir Chaal, Eugenia Ong, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked about a histone mark in the malaria parasite. In Plasmodium falciparum, chemical marks on histones help control gene activity.
