Those marks have been linked to the parasite's surface virulence factors, which it swaps to evade the human immune system.

The team asked whether one mark, a single methyl group on histone 3, has a second job. A moonlighting function would mean the same marked protein does unrelated work elsewhere. Such dual roles complicate, and enrich, the story of gene control in malaria.
plos-pone-0010352:
Yannick Muller and co-workers tested a drug pair for transplant tolerance in PLOS ONE in 2010. They moved insulin-making islet cells from rats into mice, a hard cross-species jump. Two treatments were already known to help such grafts last: an antibody against CD154, and rapamycin. The team gave both together and asked how the graft survived. They paid special attention to regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers.

With the pair, grafts lasted longer than with either drug alone. Regulatory T cells seemed to carry much of that protection. True tolerance, where the body accepts a graft without constant drugs, is a long-sought goal. This work suggests the peacekeeper cells can be boosted on purpose. That is a hopeful route for islet treatment in diabetes.
plos-pone-0010452:
Beatrice Mwagomba and colleagues documented falling death rates as HIV care expanded in rural Malawi for PLOS ONE in 2010. The district had scaled up AIDS care, including antiretroviral treatment, to its people. The team asked whether overall deaths truly fell as services grew. They cross-checked three sources: official death registers, coffin sales, and funeral counts. Agreement among unlike sources strengthens confidence in the trend.

All signs pointed the same way: mortality dropped as treatment spread. Coffin sales are an unusual but honest proxy where records are thin. Showing that treatment saves lives at district scale supports further investment. It also gives other rural programs a cheap way to track impact. Lives saved, here, were counted three ways.
plos-pone-0010552:
Catalina Pimiento and colleagues identified an ancient nursery ground for the giant shark megalodon in Panama in PLOS ONE in 2010. Modern sharks raise pups in shallow, food-rich nurseries that shelter the young. Such areas show many juveniles and newborns in the fossil or living record. Whether extinct giants used nurseries was an open question. The team studied Miocene fossils from Panama with that question in mind.

Teeth and other remains there skewed heavily toward young megalodons. That pattern marks the site as a nursery used millions of years ago. Nursery use may be an ancient shark habit, not a modern novelty. It also tells paleontologists where to seek young specimens. Even apex predators, it seems, started life in sheltered shallows.
plos-pone-0010652:
Nadia Scantlebury and colleagues linked a scaffolding protein to behavior in fruit fly larvae, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, RanBPM, organizes signaling in many cell types. In flies it was known mostly for roles in egg development.

The team showed RanBPM works inside the mushroom body, the fly brain's learning center. Larvae with altered RanBPM behaved differently in simple choice tasks. Normal amounts in that one brain area restored normal behavior. The result ties a general signaling scaffold to a specific behavior, using a brain small enough to map completely.
plos-pone-0010752:
Alexander Choukèr and colleagues studied motion sickness and the body's cannabis-like system, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many people face nausea and vomiting during travel by road, air, or sea. Motion sickness is stressful, yet the brain pathways behind it stayed murky. The endocannabinoid system helps regulate stress and nausea elsewhere in the body.

Volunteers prone to motion sickness were tested under motion stress. Their endocannabinoid levels and stress hormones shifted in telling patterns. People with stronger system responses coped better with the same motion. The link suggests new anti-nausea drugs could work by tuning this system rather than sedating the whole brain.
plos-pone-0010852:
Changhui Mao, Miao Wang, Biquan Luo and co-authors published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. GRP94 is one of the most common helper proteins inside the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop, where it assists other proteins into shape. Earlier work tied it to embryo growth, immune sensing, cancer, and autoimmune disease.

The team engineered mice with a targeted flaw in the Grp94 gene, allowing the gene to be removed fully or only in chosen tissues. Mice carrying one working copy stayed viable and became a tool for probing how cells handle folding stress. Cells from these animals showed disturbed stress signaling when the workshop was overloaded. Mao and colleagues provide a lasting mouse resource, and evidence that trimming one helper protein can unsettle the whole folding system.
plos-pone-0010952:
Max Lataillade, Jennifer Chiarella, Rong Yang and co-authors published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some people carry drug-resistant HIV before ever taking treatment, having caught a resistant strain. Standard tests miss resistant viruses present in tiny amounts, so the team used ultra-deep sequencing on stored samples from the CASTLE treatment trial.

They compared patients whose treatment failed within a year with matched patients whose virus stayed suppressed. Deep sequencing found transmitted resistance mutations in about a third of participants, and in roughly half of those cases the mutation lurked in only a small slice of the virus population. Rates were similar across viral subtypes and treatment outcomes. Lataillade and colleagues show that hidden, low-level resistance is common before treatment, a fact that shapes how baseline testing should be done.
plos-pone-0011052:
Maria Letizia Giardino Torchia, Elena Ciaglia, Anna Maria Masci and co-authors published this HIV drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV protease inhibitors block the virus's assembly enzyme, but they also reshape immune responses by routes unrelated to the virus. The authors examined how five of these drugs affect the making of dendritic cells, the instructors of the immune system, and their dialogue with natural killer cells.

Blood monocytes from healthy donors were grown toward dendritic cells in the presence of each drug. The drugs differed in effect, but several produced immature cells with lowered display and co-stimulatory molecules, and one in particular prevented normal maturation and cytokine release. Torchia and colleagues map an off-target immune footprint of a major drug class. That footprint may explain some side effects and could be exploited to calm unwanted inflammation.
plos-pone-0011152:
Liu, Barchowsky and Opresko studied a toxic metal in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chromium in one form is a workplace and pollution hazard that damages DNA. The damage is worst at telomeres, the caps that protect chromosome ends, especially when cells copy their DNA under stress.

They found a protein linked to a premature aging syndrome guards those caps against chromium driven harm. That protective role connects pollution exposure to aging biology. It helps explain how a common toxin may speed cell aging. The finding informs safety limits and research on how cells defend their chromosome ends.
plos-pone-0011252:
Ahmed and Santosh profiled blood metals in early Parkinson disease for PLOS ONE in 2010. Parkinson disease develops silently for years before tremor appears. The team measured metals in serum and mapped genetic linkage data, hunting for a marker that shows up early in the illness.

Aluminum emerged as a possible marker for early diagnosis. A blood based clue available early could let treatment start sooner, when it may do most good. The authors present the marker as a lead needing confirmation in larger groups. Still, the combined metal and gene approach offers a fresh route to early detection.
plos-pone-0011352:
Yacine Kharraz and co-authors reported in 2010 that making too much of one RNA-handling protein disrupts mouse embryo growth. The protein, called TIAR, moves between the cell nucleus and the surrounding fluid. In the nucleus it helps choose how RNA messages are cut and joined, and outside it can block those messages from being read into protein.

Mice engineered to produce extra TIAR showed impaired development as embryos. The harm shows that the amount of this regulator matters, not just its presence. Too much of a normal protein can bend the whole program of early growth off course. Developmental biologists can use the finding to understand dosage-sensitive steps in embryo formation. It also warns that gene activity must be tuned within narrow limits for a healthy start to life.
plos-pone-0011452:
Gary Lupyan and Michael Spivey showed in 2010 that words help the eyes find faint objects, while pictures do not help in the same way. Spotting a barely visible target is hard, and common sense says any hint should help. The team gave volunteers either a verbal cue naming the target or a visual cue showing it, then measured how fast the target was found.

Verbal cues sharpened detection clearly, but visual cues gave no such boost. That asymmetry reveals that language tunes perception in a way mere images cannot, perhaps by priming the right features in advance. The quirk has practical reach, from how warning signs are worded to how search teams are briefed. For mind science, it is clean evidence that words reach down into seeing itself, not just into thinking about what was seen.
plos-pone-0011552:
Karin Forsberg and co-authors reported in 2010 that misfolded SOD1 protein appears in the common form of ALS, not only in the inherited form. Most ALS cases are sporadic, with no SOD1 gene mutation, while a minority inherit a faulty SOD1 gene whose protein clumps. The team made new antibodies that recognize only the bent, non-native form of the protein, wherever it occurs.

Using those tools, they found inclusions of misfolded SOD1 in tissue from sporadic ALS patients. The usual suspect thus stands accused in the common form of the disease too, widening the target for treatments aimed at SOD1. Therapies being built for the genetic form might serve the far larger sporadic group. The study also shows the value of conformation-specific antibodies, tools that see a protein's shape, not just its presence.
plos-pone-0011652:
Stephen Stanhope wrote a methods paper on planning genome surveys of whole microbial communities, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such metagenomics projects sequence mixed DNA from soil or water rather than one genome. Classic maths for single-genome coverage does not answer how much sequencing a mixed sample needs.

Stanhope adapts occupancy models and calculates the odds of obtaining long unbroken sequence stretches at different effort levels. Those calculations let labs design experiments with a chosen chance of success instead of guessing. Smarter design saves money and yields community data that can actually answer the questions asked.
plos-pone-0011752:
Yuping Lin and co-authors mapped the alcohol-making enzyme system of an unusual yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The alcohol dehydrogenase system governs sugar metabolism in yeast, covering both ethanol production and use, plus the balancing of chemical cofactors. Candida maltosa can ferment glucose and also xylose, a sugar locked in plant waste that most yeasts cannot touch.

Their detailed map of this yeast's enzyme system explains part of its unusual feeding range. That toolkit interests biofuel researchers, who want microbes that turn crop leftovers into ethanol instead of competing with food crops for sugar.
plos-pone-0011852:
Sharyn Rossi and co-workers reported in 2010 on transplanting young motor nerve cells into rats with injured spinal cords. Cervical cord injury kills motor neurons, the cells that carry movement commands, and that loss drives much of the lasting weakness. The team prepared a pure batch of motor neuron progenitors, cells able to mature into motor neurons.

After transplant, the researchers checked both the tissue under the microscope and how well the animals functioned. They report gains on both counts, suggesting the grafted cells survived and supported repair in the injured cord. Results of this kind are early, but they test whether replacing lost motor neurons is a realistic route toward restoring movement.
plos-pone-0011952:
Nathan Dees and Sonya Bahar used a computer model in 2010 to ask how big a mutation should be for new species to form fastest. Work on mutation rates had already shown that evolution tunes how often changes occur. The related question of change size, how far a single mutation moves a trait, had received less attention.

In their simple evolutionary model, mutation size itself had an optimum for speciation. Steps too small creep without splitting populations; steps too large overshoot workable forms. A middle size splits one population into two most readily. Model results like this guide how biologists think about the raw material that real genomes supply to evolution.
plos-pone-0012052:
Ramakrishna Sompallae and co-workers profiled in 2010 the gene activity of cells making a key Epstein-Barr virus protein. EBNA-1 keeps the virus's genome going, regulates its genes, and helps reshape the cell during the virus-driven immortalization that can lead to cancer. Its cellular targets were only partly known.

Transcription profiling of cells expressing EBNA-1 suggested the protein targets chromatin remodeling complexes, the machinery that opens and closes DNA. If a viral protein steers the host's DNA packaging, it can reprogram the cell broadly from a single post. That route helps explain how EBV turns a normal B cell into a permanently growing one.
plos-pone-0012152:
Claude Nogues, Hervé Leh, Christopher Langendorf, and co-authors refined a tool for watching antibodies bind their targets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their method lays out tiny peptide spots on a chip and images binding with a light-based sensor. A stubborn problem is stray binding: molecules sticking where they should not, which blurs every measurement on the chip.

The team characterized how to keep that background low so real binding stands out. Reliable chips can screen thousands of antibody interactions at once, speeding vaccine and diagnostic work. Methods papers like this rarely make headlines, yet later discoveries quietly rest on the accuracy they establish.
plos-pone-0012252:
Maliha Zahid, Brett Phillips, Sean Albers, and co-authors hunted for a peptide that homes to the heart, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A short protein string able to enter heart tissue specifically could ferry drugs, genes, or imaging agents straight to the heart while sparing the rest of the body. They searched for such a string by screening vast peptide libraries inside living mice, keeping only what landed in heart tissue.

The search yielded a peptide segment that transduces heart tissue with unusual selectivity. Delivery is the weakest link in most heart therapies, which flood the whole body to reach one organ. A heart-specific address label could cut doses and side effects across many treatments at once.
plos-pone-0012352:
Joan Segura Mora, Salam Assi and Narcis Fernandez-Fuentes built a free web tool, described in PLOS ONE in 2010, that finds the key spots where two proteins touch. When proteins bind, only a few contact points do most of the gripping work. Drug makers prize those hot spots, because a small drug that blocks one can stop the whole interaction.

Their server, PCRPi-W, takes a protein pair's shape and predicts which contact points matter most. It charts the hot spots so users can see them at a glance. Any lab with a web browser can use it, which makes hot-spot hunting faster for drug design and for basic studies of how proteins work together.
plos-pone-0012452:
Vladislava Melnikova, Andrey Dobroff, Maya Zigler and colleagues traced a gene-silencing link in melanoma, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. As this skin cancer turns malignant, it loses a protein called AP-2 alpha while a switch protein named CREB grows more active. Whether one change drives the other was unknown.

The team showed that CREB directly represses AP-2 alpha, tying the two hallmarks into one pathway that favors malignant behavior. A single chain of cause is easier to attack than two separate mysteries. The work nominates CREB blocking as a strategy worth testing against advanced melanoma, which resists most current drugs.
plos-pone-0012552:
Rajaganapathi Jagannathan, Suma Kaveti, Russell Desnoyer and colleagues watched a hormone receptor reshape chromosome packaging, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The AT1 receptor receives angiotensin II, a blood pressure hormone, and belongs to the large GPCR receptor family. Chronic activation stresses gene regulation in vessel cells, contributing to heart and vessel disease.

The team found AT1 activation alters histone H2A, one of the spool proteins DNA wraps around, revealing a route by which GPCRs remodel chromatin. A surface receptor reaching all the way to the chromosome spools is a striking finding. It opens new angles on how blood pressure drugs and stress hormones leave lasting gene marks.
plos-pone-0012652:
Carvalho, Melo, Bruno and co-authors counted a rare immune cell type in people with a faulty antibody system. The disorder, called common variable immunodeficiency, is the most frequent cause of antibody failure in adults and children. Patients suffer repeat bacterial infections and often autoimmune problems as well.

Their 2010 blood study found the balance of activated natural killer T cells was skewed in these patients. That skew adds to a growing list of innate immune faults in the disorder. Knowing the full set of faults helps doctors sort patients and choose care.
plos-pone-0012752:
Jelsbak, Ingmer, Valihrach and co-authors traced how a helper protein raises a key surface protein of Staphylococcus aureus. The helper family, Clp chaperones, refolds and remodels other proteins in bacteria. Protein A on the staph surface helps the germ dodge immune attack and is a classic virulence factor.

Their 2010 study shows the chaperone ClpX boosts protein A through a regulator called Rot, and also by a second route. Two paths to one virulence factor make the system robust. Cutting either path could weaken a germ behind many hard infections.
plos-pone-0012852:
Inderjit, Bajpai and Rajeshwari examined how a plant chemical's fate in soil decides what it actually does. Plants release chemicals that can hold back rival plants, a process called allelopathy. Most past tests simply grew plants with the chemical and watched growth, assuming a direct effect.

Their 2010 study followed 8-hydroxyquinoline in soil and showed the soil itself mediates the chemical's action. Microbes and soil binding can weaken, change or concentrate such compounds. Field claims for plant warfare need that soil step included, or they mislead.  Soil samples came from the plant's own growing ground.
plos-pone-0329052:
Liang Fang, Chengxiang Li, and Chen Jin tested whether China's new urbanization strategy, a national push for better-integrated city growth, raises both the amount and the quality of green innovation in cities. Panel data covered two hundred eighty-four cities from 2011 to 2022. Statistical models with city and year controls separated the policy's effect from background trends.

Urbanization reform significantly boosted both the quantity of green innovation and its quality. The effect grew stronger where digital inclusive finance combined with government technology support, better information infrastructure, stronger regional economies, and particular energy patterns. In other words, city reform works best when finance and technology ecosystems move with it. The results guide where complementary investment will multiply the policy's green return.
plos-pone-0339752:
Sissel Groth and co-authors explored why nurses underuse video consultations in Danish heart clinics. Video visits are spreading, yet nurses' uncertainty can stall them. Their 2026 qualitative study ran two focus groups with nurses from two cardiology outpatient clinics and read the material interpretively.

Three themes organised the nurses' experience. Timing came first: video must be used at the right moment, for the right patient and purpose. The nurse-patient relationship itself changed shape on screen, in ways nurses were still learning to read. Organisational backing, from scheduling to technical help, decided whether good intentions survived the clinic day. Groth and colleagues list the prerequisites nurses say managers must supply.
plos-pone-0343652:
Ling Huang and Yunqing Zhang analyze English-language news about a Chinese grass technology spread across developing countries to grow mushrooms and feed stock. The method is praised for yields, poverty relief, and land repair, yet headlines shape whether farmers and officials adopt it. Using automated topic and emotion tools on a self-built news collection from over a dozen countries across recent years, the team mapped themes and feelings.

Five themes dominated, from government-led training to global partnership framing. Positive feelings ruled overall, with trust and hopeful anticipation strongest; negative feelings aimed at poverty and hunger themselves, casting the technology as the fix. Huang and Zhang argue that such warm framing quietly does adoption work that field results alone cannot.
plos-pone-0344552:
Bethany Stanley and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One case-control study asking whether how quickly mothers and babies answer each other's sounds predicts later psychiatric diagnosis. Videos of mother-infant interaction from a large British birth cohort were analyzed for response timing, and children were assessed for disorders at age seven: fifty-five cases and just over one hundred controls.

The sweet spot for counting a maternal reply was about one second, and for the baby about eight seconds. Only the mothers' responsiveness predicted later diagnosis, and the link was confined to hyperactivity and conduct disorders, holding regardless of the mother's education or the child's sex. Babies' own response timing showed no such link. The authors suggest such precise early measures could help target support to families most likely to benefit.
plos-pone-0345152:
Fatima Muse and seven colleagues pool studies on high uric acid in preeclampsia across poorer countries. Their 2026 systematic review searched four databases for hospital studies from 2010 to 2025. Elevated uric acid is a classic laboratory companion of this dangerous pregnancy disorder. But reported frequencies swung widely between settings. Eleven studies covering just under eleven hundred women in seven countries qualified. A random-effects model combined their prevalence estimates.

About half the women with preeclampsia had hyperuricemia, the pooled figure landing near fifty-three percent. Studies agreed with each other reasonably well. Their blood thresholds for calling uric acid high, however, ranged noticeably. That definitional drift is itself a finding. Clinicians in low-resource hospitals often lean on cheap tests like uric acid. Knowing the true frequency, and the threshold problem, helps them judge how much weight one number deserves when deciding how sick a mother is.
plos-pone-0345252:
Yejun Soun, Hosung Lee, and U Kang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It tackles stock movement prediction, forecasting whether share prices will rise or fall. Their method aims for accuracy, a hard goal in markets swayed by noise and sudden news.

The technique is called centroid-based randomness smoothing. In plain terms, it steadies predictions by averaging over many slightly varied versions of the input data, grouped around central patterns. More stable forecasts are less likely to flip on random jitter in the data. Quantitative traders and machine learning researchers testing prediction methods are the audience for this approach.
plos-pone-0347052:
Ruishi Liang, Shuo Li, and Shuaibing Li built a small vision model that spots smoking on work sites. A lit cigarette is a fire risk on a building site. But a cigarette is tiny, and site photos are full of clutter. Most light models miss it.

Their model, AOW-YOLO, tweaks a known light design in three ways. It scores its own errors in a smarter way. It keeps more fine detail when it shrinks an image. And it swaps in a leaner core. On test data it beat rival light models. It also ran about a third faster than the base design it grew from.
plos-pone-0347652:
Johan Ljunggren and seven colleagues ask how declining kidney function reshapes the body's chemistry. Their 2026 study draws on three Swedish population cohorts, over thirty-four hundred people in total. Kidneys normally clear many small molecules from the blood. When they weaken, those molecules pile up. Some may help explain why kidney problems raise heart disease risk.

Mass spectrometry measured nearly eight hundred metabolites per person. Ninety-six metabolites tracked kidney function consistently across discovery and validation samples. The team then used genetic methods to probe which links might be causal. Their adjustments accounted for body fat, diabetes, medicines, and heart risk factors. The catalogue gives researchers concrete candidate molecules for explaining the kidney-heart connection, rather than vague suspicion about waste build-up.
plos-pone-0347852:
Lai-Ying Zhang and colleagues take a single-cell census of lung wash fluid in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Bronchoalveolar lavage, a rinse of the airways, is a routine test in interstitial lung disease, a family of scarring lung conditions, but its cells had never been profiled one by one.

Profiling samples from twenty-four men with conditions including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, and silicosis revealed sixteen distinct cell populations, with macrophage subgroups following diverging paths between diseases. The team also checked whether short telomeres, the chromosome caps tied to fibrosis risk, changed the picture, and cross-referenced the data with genetic studies. Such maps could sharpen diagnosis, since lavage is already collected in clinic.
plos-pone-0348352:
Kai Zhao and co-workers search for faulty gene changes behind a disorder of the tiny hairs that sweep mucus through airways. About half of patients with this disorder also have organs mirrored left to right. Their 2026 study reads the full gene set of three unrelated patients and checks one suspect gene closely, modeling how each change would disturb its protein.

Seven suspect changes turned up in that gene, all at spots evolution kept unchanged. Each patient carried a matched pair, one from each parent, fitting the disease pattern. The changes were predicted to weaken the protein and bend its shape. The cases widen the known list of changes in this gene and can sharpen genetic counseling for affected families.
plos-pone-0348952:
Aihua Li and colleagues asked whether a simple combined index of belly fat and blood fats predicts death risk in younger adults with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes is rising fast in young adults, and this cardiometabolic index blends waist and height with triglycerides and protective cholesterol. The team followed more than two thousand Americans aged twenty to sixty-five from national survey data.

Those with higher index values died more often, from all causes and from cardiovascular causes in particular, and the relationship rose in a straight line rather than a curve. Splitting the data into subgroups did not change the picture. A cheap index built from routine measures could help doctors spot the young patients who need the closest watching.
plos-pone-0349252:
Lv and colleagues, in a 2026 study, measure how hot industrial slag particles trade heat with air inside a spinning heat exchanger. Steelworks pour off molten slag in huge amounts, and granulating it while recovering its heat could save energy. The exchanger blows cold air against the falling hot particles. Two slags were compared: blast furnace slag alone, and steelmaking slag mixed with metal bits.

In tests backed by computer simulation, the exchanger reached its best efficiency under a sweet spot of settings, recovering most of the heat for the pure slag. The mixed slag did slightly worse, and the more metal bits it held, the worse it got. Where particles spread inside the chamber mattered a great deal to the result. The authors give designers a clearer basis for sizing and running such exchangers, a step toward steel plants that harvest their own waste heat.
plos-pone-0349352:
Shane Guenin and four colleagues test a basic assumption of airport wildlife management in this 2026 meta-analysis. Managers spend heavily to reduce bird numbers near runways. The logic seems obvious: more birds nearby should mean more collisions with aircraft. Yet nobody had checked the evidence across studies. The team searched the literature and pooled the results.

Thirteen studies provided twenty usable effect sizes. Across them, bird abundance and strike frequency did move together, with a moderate positive correlation. That supports the standard management approach. But the evidence base looks shaky. Studies disagreed a lot with each other, and signs of publication bias appeared. Statistical power was low, and methods varied widely. The tenet survives the test, though the authors urge better-designed studies before airports stake even more money on it.
plos-pone-0349852:
Manigandan Chockalingam and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE laying out a planned review of what patients themselves say about relative motion orthoses. These finger splints protect healing tendons and joints while still letting the hand move and be used, and earlier reviews focused on clinical results rather than daily-life experience. The planned review will gather studies reporting how acceptable the splints feel, how easy they are to use, and how they affect everyday activities.

The protocol follows established scoping review methods, with searches across major medical databases plus dissertations and other grey literature. Two reviewers will screen and extract the patient-perspective data independently, with a third settling disagreements, and no formal quality scoring is planned. The project is registered openly in advance. The finished map is meant to show clinicians and designers where patient experience evidence is rich, and where it is missing.
plos-pone-0349952:
Omar Hafidi and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of wheat roots. It asks how wheat variety shapes the bacteria living around and inside roots. It also asks how that links to resisting Fusarium root rot. Four varieties with known grades of tolerance were grown and compared. The team studied root shape and root chemistry. They also mapped the microbes in the soil near roots and in root tissue.

The most tolerant variety, Concret, grew roots whose traits lined up with more helpful bacteria. Those bacteria included Bacillus and Lysobacter. Chemical tests found a small set of root compounds that set the varieties apart. Those compounds also tracked with certain bacterial groups. The authors argue that breeding for root traits could steer root microbes toward protection. That would offer a living complement to chemical disease control.
plos-pone-0350452:
Laura Bravo-Merodio and co-authors used UK Biobank data in 2026 to ask why schooling seems to protect thinking skills in later life. One idea is that education strengthens brain networks through a chemical messenger system linked to alertness.

Machine learning and mediation tests combined genes for that messenger system, brain scans of a front-to-side network, and test scores. Education and biology together explained thinking scores better than either alone. Links within the right side of that network carried much of education's effect. The results hint that lifelong learning may protect the mind partly by keeping key brain connections strong.
plos-pone-0350552:
Jennifer S Albrecht and co-authors published the plan for RETRO-TBI in 2026, a study of mild brain injury in older adults. This age group suffers the most hospitalisations and deaths from head injury, yet recovery in later life is the least studied. No results are reported yet.

Two hundred fifty people aged sixty-five and over will be followed at home for a year after injury, across body, mind, mood, and sleep. Blood samples at each visit support biomarker work. The aims trace recovery paths and their predictors within and across domains. The design treats recovery as several linked journeys, not one score.
plos-pone-0350652:
Yingyang Li and colleagues studied delirium, a sudden state of confusion, in intensive care patients in 2026. They focused on a blood measure that compares stress-driven high sugar with a person's usual sugar level, asking whether that ratio predicts who becomes delirious.

Records for more than two thousand intensive care patients were reviewed. The link was not a straight line: below a low turning point the ratio mattered little, but above it the odds of delirium rose sharply. Certain patient groups showed a stronger link than others. If confirmed, a simple ratio from routine blood tests could flag patients who need closer watching and early care.
plos-pone-0350952:
Danail Georgiev Ivanov and Petar Peev studied nineteen players from FC NSA Sofia Women, the Bulgarian women's football champions. Their cross-sectional screening study appeared in 2026. They measured knee strength with a handheld device. They also compared hamstring strength against quadriceps strength. Two kinds of vertical jump were recorded, with both legs and with one leg, broken down by playing position.

Almost every player tested had at least one leg where hamstrings fell below the usual balance mark. More than half also jumped unevenly between legs in the single-leg squat jump. The authors argue that regular balance and jump checks belong in elite women's training. They also say conditioning should build hamstrings and quadriceps together, rather than chasing hamstring strength alone.
plos-pone-0351152:
B Vishnu Vardhana Naidu and co-authors tested cleaner fuel mixes for diesel-type engines in 2026. They blended two plant-based biodiesel fuels, from juliflora and kapok, and added hydrogen, a fuel with high energy for its weight, to see how the engine behaved.

One blend with hydrogen raised heat efficiency and power measures while cutting fuel use and most exhaust gases, including carbon monoxide and smoke. One harmful gas, nitrogen oxides, rose, which is the trade-off to solve. Computer methods helped find the best mix and predict performance. The work supports pairing hydrogen with waste-plant fuels for transport that pollutes less.
plos-pone-0351252:
Edwin Estomii Ngowi and Angela M Jesse judged a farm support project for villages along the Mara River in Tarime District, Tanzania. The project pushed climate smart farming, new income options, and fairer roles for women. Evidence came from more than two hundred and fifty small farmers, group talks, key interviews, and project papers.

Three quarters of farmers had taken up methods that cope better with a changing climate. Most villages had drawn up plans that respond to womens needs, and about two thirds of homes added side incomes like poultry or bees. Yet poor access to markets held sales back, and custom still limited how fully women could join in. Lasting gains will need roads to buyers and shifts in social rules, not farm training alone.
plos-pone-0351352:
Margo Gustina and Robert Berrens published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its title states the theme: voters reveal public library value. The evidence comes from United States referendums, public votes where communities decide directly whether to fund their libraries.

Referendum results are honest measures of value because voters back them with their own taxes. Economists struggle to price public goods people do not buy in shops, and library votes offer rare real numbers. Library advocates and local officials preparing funding measures are the readers for evidence drawn from actual ballots.
plos-pone-0351552:
George Reiss and six colleagues report results for a glaucoma procedure in this 2026 study. Open-angle glaucoma slowly strangles vision when eye pressure stays high. The procedure opens a drainage cleft inside the eye with a microsurgical cannula. It then reinforces that cleft with a sliver of donated scleral tissue, a first-of-its-kind implant. Forty-one eyes from thirty-eight patients were followed prospectively across several centres. Two-thirds had resisted earlier treatment.

A year out, the numbers looked strong. Mean eye pressure had fallen by thirty-one percent, landing inside the normal range. Medication counts, complications, and any need for more glaucoma surgery were tracked as well. Most eyes were hard cases, including failed previous operations. Real-world evidence matters because surgical innovations often shine in trials and fade in ordinary clinics. A standalone, implant-supported drainage route could widen options for patients running out of them.
plos-pone-0351652:
Shots that guard against human papillomavirus prevent cancers, yet safety worries slow uptake. Siqi Zhang and colleagues mined the United States vaccine side-effect reporting system for reports filed after these shots between 2006 and 2024, in this 2026 PLOS One analysis.

Nearly seventy-eight thousand reports were included, most about girls and women, and almost half about people under eighteen. Headache and tiredness appeared most; fainting was the most common strong signal, and a heart-rhythm condition showed the strongest statistical link. Most reports came within a month of the shot. The authors note such reports show patterns to study, not proof the vaccine caused each event.
plos-pone-0351752:
Boris Camiletti and colleagues studied California avocados to learn when fruit should be picked so it ripens well without rotting. They tracked ten varieties, including Hass and several newer types, across seasons. The team measured dry matter, the usual sign of maturity, and watched for stem rot, body rot, and streaking inside the fruit during storage.

Lab work named the fungi behind the decay, mostly species of Neofusicoccum, plus Colletotrichum and Diaporthe. One Neofusicoccum species proved the most damaging in tests on fruit. Dry matter rose in clear seasonal patterns, and for some varieties it helped predict disease. The results support setting both lowest and highest maturity limits for picking, not just a minimum.
plos-pone-0351952:
Nyagawa and colleagues asked relatives of hospital patients in Dar es Salaam about donating a kidney in a 2026 study. Transplant beats dialysis for kidney failure, but Tanzania relies on living relatives as donors. More than four hundred relatives at the national hospital answered questions on knowledge, attitudes, and willingness.

Willingness was low overall, and most relatives lacked solid knowledge about donation. A positive attitude raised willingness sharply, while older age, being female, and informal work each lowered it. Teaching programs that build accurate knowledge and address fears could widen the donor pool. Without more willing relatives, many patients will stay on dialysis far longer than needed.
plos-pone-0352152:
Di Feng and four colleagues published this 2026 study of China's Grand Canal in Huai'an, where an old working waterway is being remade as a cultural attraction. The team surveyed how visitors perceive the canal's heritage value and what experiences they want, then used correlation analysis to map how the two sets of views connect.

The link proved uneven rather than simple: storytelling value and the spirit of the place drove demand for educational experiences especially hard. Feng proposes a dynamic model for turning industrial heritage into living cultural space without freezing it in the past.
plos-pone-0352252:
Ellen Kuipers and colleagues sorted people preparing for weight-loss surgery into groups by their behavior and state of mind, rather than treating them as one uniform crowd. Questionnaires before surgery covered health, quality of life, social support, eating habits, and mood for two hundred seventy-two patients. A statistical method then let natural clusters emerge from the answers.

Four profiles appeared. The largest, nearly half, reported no real deficits in any area. Another group paired decent emotional health with weaker physical functioning and problem eating, and the remaining profiles mixed struggles in different proportions. Knowing which profile a patient fits could help clinics aim support where it is needed, extra eating-behavior help for one person, mood care for another, instead of giving everyone the same preparation.
plos-pone-0352352:
Ritbano Ahmed Abdo and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One scoping review from Ethiopia. It covers research on contraception offered to mothers right after birth. The focus is long-acting methods like implants and coils. These methods prevent closely spaced pregnancies. But the Ethiopian proof base is scattered. The reviewers charted forty-two studies from databases and grey sources.

Reported uptake ranged widely. It ran from about a fifth to just over half of mothers. Personal, service, and family factors shaped the choice. Most studies were one-time surveys centered on women. Few looked at partners, at whole towns, or at lived experience. The authors call for stronger, more inclusive study designs. Such work would support true shared decisions after birth.
plos-pone-0352452:
Qin and Lee traced how talk about Fukushima wastewater changed on Chinese social media in a 2026 study. Japan's plan to release treated water from the damaged plant drew both safety worries and anger tied to national pride. The team sorted themes in more than fifty thousand posts on Weibo, a large Chinese platform.

Early posts mixed technical and safety talk with patriotic claims, but patriotic talk soon took over. Ordinary users drove most of that shift, voicing anger at Japan rooted in past wars and wider distrust of Western powers. Well-known posters stayed more technical, though some boosted anti-Western claims, which shows how a safety issue became a test of loyalty.
plos-pone-0352752:
Andrea Salas-Ortiz and seven colleagues ask whether a manager's own character shapes how well HIV clinics are run. This matters in Eswatini, where clinics serving key groups work under real money strain. The 2026 study covers forty-five community sites and their managers. Each manager filled a standard Big Five inventory. Management strength was scored from site records and direct checks. Records also captured each site's size, age, and funding.

Sites sorted into two clusters by how they were run. Sites in the stronger cluster differed clearly in how strongly they were led. Their money and people handling stood out as the main gap. Traits like openness and warmth tagged along with the stronger cluster. Who runs a clinic, it turns out, may shape the care it gives. Training that stops at buildings and budgets misses the person in charge.
plos-pone-0353352:
Han Gao and four colleagues hunt for genes that link the cell's recycling system, autophagy, to atherosclerosis, the artery-clogging disease behind most heart attacks and strokes, in this 2026 study. They mined four public gene expression datasets from patients and controls. They crossed the results with a catalogue of autophagy-related genes, then used machine learning and protein network analysis to narrow the field.

Five genes survived validation in two further datasets as characteristic markers of the disease, and their activity tracked with immune cell patterns in the tissue. Follow-up experiments in animal and cell models singled out one of them, CASP1, which ran high in diseased samples. The authors present CASP1, best known for driving inflammation, as a promising candidate for future drug work, alongside the regulatory networks they mapped around all five genes.
plos-pone-0353552:
Elena Kukhar and four colleagues published this 2026 veterinary study of three captive steppe eagles in Kazakhstan. All three birds suffered chronic bumblefoot, a stubborn footpad disease that had not healed with antibacterial drugs. The team sampled the deep lesions and identified the culprit with lab, chemical, and gene tests.

Every isolate proved to be Candida metapsilosis, a yeast that can feed on keratin and tolerate heat. The sores healed once targeted antifungal treatment began, supporting a real role for the yeast. Kukhar advises checking for fungi whenever raptor foot wounds refuse to close.
plos-pone-0353652:
Hadi Rezaei and seven colleagues chart bee, wasp, and hornet stings in northwestern Iran, in this 2026 PLOS ONE review of hospital records from 2021 to 2024. Two hundred and twenty-five patients treated across East Azerbaijan Province were analysed for who gets stung, where on the body, and when. Most patients were male, and cases peaked both in young children and in working-age adults.

Summer brought over half the stings, and the head and neck were the commonest sites — a pattern the authors link to clothing customs and work habits. Slightly more incidents happened in towns than in the countryside. The authors recommend household awareness campaigns and protective clothing for outdoor workers, tuned to local dress and jobs.
plos-pone-0353852:
Dongming Gao and three colleagues test a familiar blood-pressure drug as a possible treatment after brain injury, in a 2026 study on rats. No effective therapy exists for the memory and thinking problems that follow traumatic brain injury. Earlier work hinted that propranolol might help, and the team suspected the brain's waste-clearing network, the glymphatic system, was involved.

Rats with a controlled injury to the brain's surface scored better on thinking tests after propranolol treatment, and their waste-clearing function recovered. Harmful protein deposits fell, damaged wiring was better preserved, and a key water channel in brain support cells increased. Blocking two molecules in the same signaling chain produced similar benefits, supporting the idea that the drug works by calming that chain. The results point to a cheap, well-known drug worth testing further.
plos-pone-0353952:
Mehrbanoo Kazemi Alamouti and seven colleagues catalogue the brain chemicals that control feeding in a major wheat pest, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The sunn pest, Eurygaster integriceps, devastates grain across the Middle East and Central Asia. The team examined thirteen feeding-related neuropeptides — small signalling molecules — charting their structures and where and when each is switched on in the insect's body.

Most were far more active in the head than the gut, fitting a command role in the brain, and many ran higher in males than females. Activity peaked early in life. The atlas gives pest scientists precise targets: blocking one such signal might stop the pest feeding without broad-spectrum poisons.
plos-pone-0354152:
Bibi Hajira and three colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for mapping research on mental health around childbirth among women who moved to Canada from South Asia. Pregnancy and the year after birth are risky times for mental health, and migration can add isolation, stigma, and language barriers. South Asian women form one of Canada's largest and fastest-growing immigrant groups, yet their evidence base has never been gathered in one place.

The planned review will search five databases plus government and community sources for work published since 2000. It will chart outcomes, risk and protective factors, and the paths women take to find help. The map is meant to expose gaps for researchers and policymakers.
plos-pone-0354252:
Huang and Li, in a 2026 safety review, gather what is known about side effects of camrelizumab, a cancer immunotherapy drug used mainly in China. Real-world safety reports are scarce, so the team mined the World Health Organization's global side effect database and published case reports from the drug's first years on the market.

Six hundred reports sat in the global database, nearly all from Asian patients and most from men. Blood problems led the list, including bone marrow suppression and low platelet counts, followed by skin reactions such as rash and itching. A growth of tiny blood vessels on the skin is a signature side effect of this drug. Rare but serious events included heart muscle inflammation and severe blistering skin reactions. Case reports added timing: effects appeared a median of eight weeks in. The authors give clinicians a watch list, stressing blood counts, skin, and heart checks.
plos-pone-0354352:
Emile Charles, Suzanne Soares-Wynter, and Shu Ng survey in 2026 what primary school children in Jamaica drink, and how school surroundings shape those choices. About nine hundred children aged seven to eleven reported their drink habits, tastes, and knowledge, while audits covered the food setting inside and outside their thirty schools. Sweet drinks are common in Jamaica and schools occupy much of a child's day.

A fifth of children reported not drinking water at all. Child level factors shaped every drink type, while outside school factors weighed heaviest for sweet drinks and classroom rules mattered more for unsweetened drinks. The authors back school rules that promote plain drinks and discourage sweet ones.
plos-pone-0354452:
Ubukata and colleagues, in a 2026 study, teach artificial intelligence to spot retinitis pigmentosa in eye photographs. This inherited disease slowly kills the light-sensing cells of the retina and can end in blindness. Early signs are easy to miss, yet photos of the back of the eye are taken at routine checkups all the time and rarely screened for it.

The team fine-tuned three image models that had first learned general vision tasks, using about three hundred photos from a Tokyo-area university hospital. The best model matched the average accuracy of eye doctors, sorting patients from healthy subjects correctly in nearly every case. Heat maps of its attention showed it looked at the outer retina and the rear pole of the eye, areas where this disease leaves its marks. The authors propose the tool as a screening assistant that flags suspect photos for a doctor's closer look.
plos-pone-0354752:
Ling Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 smart grid study of sorting households by their daily electricity use patterns, which utilities need for demand programs. Labeled examples are scarce, so their system, GridCL, learns from unlabeled data by comparing slightly altered versions of each day's usage curve.

Across anonymized data from three cities, the method grouped users well and, with only a tenth of users labeled, classified new ones accurately and steadily. Zhang presents self-teaching on raw meter data as a practical answer to the label shortage.
plos-pone-0354952:
Sukrit Narula and co-authors examine in 2026 whether inherited risk can spot high blood pressure missed in clinic visits. They studied younger adults in Liechtenstein who took part in a population health project. Two kinds of inherited clues were compared: a combined genetic score and simple family history.

Daytime pressure measured away from the clinic was tied to both clues, yet the two clues barely overlapped with each other. Adding the genetic score slightly improved a proven prediction tool, while family history added almost nothing. The authors stress the gain was modest, so wider work is needed before such scores help in everyday care.
plos-pone-0355552:
Sebastian Arrizabalaga and co-authors test in 2026 a new way to prepare human neural stem cells for an eye disease that wastes the central retina. They compared the older cell mix with a fresh single cell suspension in rats bred for retinal decline. Cells were placed under the retina in one eye, with salt solution in the other.

Both cell forms survived in place and kept nearby light sensing layers thicker. The new form spread more widely and gave better vision test results. Because the study bridges toward human trials, the finding matters for plans to treat a common cause of sight loss in older adults.
plos-pone-0355652:
Xiaoyuan Weng and colleagues examined in 2026 how fairly a risk score for triple-negative breast cancer holds up when it is tested across different patient groups. The score is built around mitochondrial proteostasis, the upkeep of protein quality inside the cell's energy factories. plos-pone-0355952:

Their symptoms are often invisible and poorly captured by standard tests.

Participants most often reported anxiety, depression, sleep problems, brain fog, and fatigue, and many had cut back or stopped working. Encounters with dismissive clinicians left deep marks, while being believed transformed experiences for the better. People described researching wellness treatments on their own more than following provider suggestions. plos-pone-0356052:

Their 2026 survey reached psychiatrists in government, university, and private care.

About four in five respondents had experienced at least one patient suicide, often early in their careers. Most rated the emotional impact high, and over half said their clinical confidence suffered. Women reported a stronger sense of personal responsibility than men. Almost none took time off, and few sought outside support. The authors call for clear procedures, supportive leadership, and peer support after such deaths.
plos-pone-0357452:

Models that combined traits beat single-trait models by a wide margin, and sites differed in how well they predicted each other. Each breeding cycle gained a modest step in grain yield while plants grew slightly shorter. Bajgain and colleagues say family plots plus combined models give the young crop a workable path forward.
plos-pone-0357752:

In mice bred to model Alzheimer's, fragments from several disease-linked genes rose sharply in brain tissue, and the same rises appeared in blood exosomes. In dish-grown immune cells exposed to amyloid, one fragment in particular was packed into exosomes at very high levels, showing the loading is active, not accidental. Because exosomes protect their cargo and reflect brain chemistry, these fragments, the authors say, could become an early blood test, pending proof in human patients.
plos-pone-0357952:

These chemicals tie to nitric oxide, a signaling molecule affecting blood flow and muscle. They took muscle from healthy adults and processed pieces with or without a salt-water wash and the preservative.

Washing clearly mattered for nitrate: washed samples read much lower and agreed better with each other, while unwashed samples were noisy and biased. Nitrite readings barely differed between washed and unwashed tissue, and the preserving solution changed neither chemical's result. The authors recommend the wash as a simple reliability step, noting they did not directly measure the blood pigments involved. That should make future muscle nitric oxide studies easier to compare.

Bezhin Meadow gives peasant boys telling ghost tales by a night fire, in pages of famous beauty and dread. Landowners, overseers, and serf actors and singers fill out a survey no statistics could match for truth of life. The sportsman's mild voice let radical matter past the censor into the conscience of the reading class of Russia. Alexander II kept the book by him, it was said, when he signed emancipation.
un-ga-res-1752: West New Guinea passed from Dutch hands toward Indonesia under a deal noted in Resolution 1752, adopted on 21 September 1962. Indonesia and the Netherlands had settled their long fight over the land. The Assembly thanks the Acting Secretary-General for his work in bringing the peace about. It takes note of the deal, accepts the role the deal gives the Secretary-General, and grants him power to carry out the tasks laid on him.
un-ga-res-1952:
Hope and pressure mix in Resolution 1952, adopted by the General Assembly on 11 December 1963, on the question of Northern Rhodesia. The British-run land, soon to become Zambia, stood near the end of colonial rule. The Assembly had read the report of its decolonization team and heard the ruling power report fresh steps toward a new constitution that same month.

The text states again the fixed right of the people of Northern Rhodesia to rule themselves and stand free. It notes with pleasure that votes for a new law-making council will be held in January 1964. Britain is asked to fix, with the new elected rulers, a date for freedom, and as soon as can be. The hope is voiced that no new block will bar the way.
un-ga-res-a-69-52:
United action toward a world free of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/52, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states, it holds, must take fresh, workable steps toward the total end of such arms. The end goal of all arms work is named: full disarmament under strict and sound world check.

Deep worry at the ruinous toll of any use of nuclear arms runs through the text. All states must keep to world law at all times, the law of war among it. Every effort must be made, it holds, to shun the use of such arms at all. The vote stands in a yearly chain that keeps the end goal in sight.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 1752 (XVII) was adopted on 21 September 1962. It welcomed the settlement of the dispute over West New Guinea, also called West Irian. The dispute was between Indonesia and the Netherlands. The Assembly took note of their agreement. It praised the Acting Secretary-General's part in reaching a peaceful deal. It gave the Secretary-General power to carry out the tasks the agreement gave him.

General Assembly Resolution 1952 (XVIII), adopted on 11 December 1963, concerned Northern Rhodesia, the British-ruled territory that soon became Zambia. The Assembly restated the people's firm right to self-rule and independence, in line with the 1960 declaration on ending colonial rule.

The text welcomed word that voting for a new Legislative Council would take place in January 1964. It voiced the hope that independence would come at the nearest possible date. It asked the ruling power to fix that date, working with the newly elected government. It asked that nothing block the territory's move to statehood.

General Assembly resolution 69/52 (2014), 'United action towards the total elimination of nuclear weapons,' strings together the practical agenda of the Non-Proliferation Treaty system. It condemns the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's nuclear tests and missile launches in the strongest terms. It demands it abandon its programmes. It stresses that it can never hold nuclear-weapon state status. For the recognized nuclear powers it urges deeper cuts, test-ban ratification, and a fissile material treaty. It urges security assurances and universal safeguards. This comes ahead of the 2015 treaty review conference.
un-sc-res-1352:
Iraq's oil-for-food program let a sanctioned state sell oil to buy civilian goods, and it needed a short renewal in 2001. The Iraqi people had lived under sanctions for more than a decade. The program was a temporary measure, meant to cover civilian needs until Iraq met the Council's terms. Resolution 1352 was adopted unanimously on 1 June 2001.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the terms of Resolution 1330, the previous oil-for-food decision. Those terms would now run until 3 July 2001. That short span is the whole grant the resolution makes. The Council also stated what it intended next. New arrangements would be considered, to speed the flow of civilian goods into Iraq. At the same time, controls on goods banned under the sanctions had to grow tighter.
un-sc-res-1452:
Sanctions on the Taliban and Al-Qaida froze bank accounts around the world. Some frozen funds covered food, rent, and medicine for listed people. On 20 December 2002 the Security Council carved out a humanitarian exception. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The text amended how the asset freeze in resolutions 1267 and 1390 would work. States gained a way to release money for basic needs.

Funds could be freed when a state judged them necessary for basic expenses. Interest and contract payments could still be added to frozen accounts. The sanctions committee had to track which states used the exception. It would keep and update a list of them. The change softened a blunt tool without lifting the freeze.
un-sc-res-1552: In 2005 the Security Council added Resolution 1552 to its record, and the text is kept here through a Wikisource transcription. Formal resolutions like this one often extend or adjust an existing course of action rather than start one. Whatever its subject, the entry's worth lies in the exact official wording, preserved end to end.
un-sc-res-1652:
Côte d'Ivoire's peacekeeping operation was renewed by the Security Council on 24 January 2006. The International Working Group had issued a communiqué on 15 January backing the prime minister's road map to elections. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January 2006 was before the Council. The crisis and the blocks on reconciliation persisted from all sides, the Council said.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the mandates of the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and of the French forces supporting it to 15 December 2006. The troop movement provisions of resolution 1609 (2005) ran for the same period. The Council said it would review the mission's tasks and troop levels alongside the coming report on Liberia. The aim was free, fair, open elections no later than 31 October 2006. Progress on the road map would guide any change to the force.
un-sc-res-1752:
Georgia's observer mission was renewed after an attack in the Kodori valley on 13 April 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 January and 3 April. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force shared the work of steadying the zone. Talks on documents covering the non-use of violence and the return of refugees were near completion. Economic recovery in Abkhazia was judged badly needed.

The Council condemned the attack on villages in the upper Kodori valley and called for those behind it to be found. Both sides were told to resume dialogue and to honor the ceasefire and non-violence deals in full. The package of documents on non-violence and refugee return had to be finished without delay. The Council backed the confidence-building proposals put forward by the Group of Friends. It extended UNOMIG's mandate to 15 October 2007. Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity inside its recognized borders were restated.
un-sc-res-1852:
The inquiry into the Beirut bombing that killed former prime minister Rafiq Hariri gained a final extension on 17 December 2008. The International Independent Investigation Commission had sent its latest report. The Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to start work on 1 March 2009 at The Hague. The commission asked to run to 28 February 2009 so it could hand over without a break.

The Council welcomed the commission's report and praised the progress made on all the cases in its mandate. It extended the commission's mandate to 28 February 2009. The commission would keep investigating while shifting its operations, staff, and files to The Hague. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 4 December 2008 in support of the request. Once the tribunal opened, its prosecutor would take over the inquiry into the 14 February 2005 attack and any linked cases.
un-sc-res-1952: Adopted in 2010, Resolution 1952 is preserved in this collection as a Security Council act in record form. The transcription is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members state the situation in their shared diplomatic language, then convert it into instructions in numbered paragraphs. The entry keeps the conversion whole, which is where the Council's power lives.
un-sc-res-252:
Jerusalem's status brought Jordan's complaint before the Council in 1968. On 21 May 1968 the Council took up measures Israel had adopted in the city. The General Assembly had already told Israel to cancel such steps. Israel had instead taken more of them. The Council restated that land cannot be gained by military conquest.

It deplored Israel's failure to obey the Assembly resolutions. It held that all Israeli laws and acts meant to change Jerusalem's status are invalid. Taking land and property for that purpose cannot change the city's standing. Israel had to cancel the measures already taken. It also had to stop any further steps of that kind.
un-sc-res-452: For the year 1979, the catalog lists Resolution 452 among the Security Council's formal decisions. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-52: Three years of atomic work went on the record in Security Council Resolution 52, passed on 22 June 1948. The Atomic Energy Commission, set up by the Assembly's first vote in 1946, had sent the Council its first, second, and third reports. The Council rules that the Secretary-General send all three reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the reports goes with them, as a matter of special weight.
un-sc-res-652: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 652, which the catalog dates to 1990. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Iraq's oil-for-food program gained a short bridge in the spring of 2001. On 1 June, the Council adopted Resolution 1352 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The program let Iraq sell oil under UN control to buy civilian goods. Broad sanctions from the 1990 invasion of Kuwait stayed in place.

The text extends the current rules by about a month, to 3 July 2001. It then announces a plan for new rules. A Goods Review List would speed civilian trade. Controls on banned items would grow tighter. Oil cash would be kept inside the UN escrow account. The step led toward the revised sanctions of later months.

Frozen bank accounts can also freeze ordinary life. Resolution 1452, adopted unanimously on 20 December 2002, carved humanitarian room into the Taliban and Al-Qaida sanctions. People on the blacklist could not touch their money at all. That blocked rent, food, medicine, and legal bills, even where no terror link existed.

The text lets states release funds for basic expenses. Food, housing, medical care, taxes, utilities, and lawyers qualify. States must notify the sanctions committee first. Silence for forty-eight hours means consent. Larger extraordinary expenses need the committee's approval. Interest earned on frozen accounts stays frozen. The change kept pressure on listed terrorists while easing pointless hardship around them.

The year 1960 brought a wave of new African states to the UN. Congo won independence from Belgium that summer. Its freedom quickly slid into crisis and foreign meddling. Still, the new republic applied for membership at once. Resolution 152 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960.

Members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of the Congo. The Assembly soon did. A UN seat gave Congo legal standing during its turmoil. It also strengthened the case for the huge UN operation then deploying there. That mission tried to hold the country together. Congo's admission remains a marker of the great decolonization wave that reshaped the UN.

Weapons kept flowing to militias in Ituri and the Kivus, and on 27 July 2004 the arms embargo on armed groups in eastern Congo is renewed. A group of experts had reported on the flow. The parties, the Council found, had failed to meet its demands, and the inflow of arms kept the whole region insecure.

Acting under Chapter VII, the embargo measures are renewed until 31 July 2005. The measures would be reviewed by 1 October 2004 and regularly after that. The group of experts is re-established until 31 January 2005 to track compliance, with a written report due through the sanctions committee before 15 December 2004.

Resolution 1652, adopted on 24 January 2006, extends the UN operation in Côte d'Ivoire through most of that year. The Council had endorsed the international working group's January communiqué and the roadmap for ending the country's division. The Secretary-General's report of 3 January described a peace process still blocked by obstacles from all sides.

Under Chapter VII, the mandates of the UN operation, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it were extended until 15 December 2006. The special arrangements for reinforcing UNOCI, set the previous June, were extended for the same period. The Council voiced deep worry that the crisis dragged on, a judgment repeated so often in these renewals that it reads as the era's refrain.

Resolution 1752, passed on 13 April 2007, keeps the UN watch team in Georgia for six more months. Two UN reports, in January and April, set out the team's work in Abkhazia. The Council praised the UN chief and his envoy for their steady push. A friends group, Russia as go-between, and a European security body all lent a hand. The team worked hand in glove with a peace force from the post-Soviet bloc, and both held the zone calm.

The team's term ran to October 2007. The Council restated its faith in Georgia's unity and its borders, as the world knows them. A pact could come by calm means alone, it said. Both sides were called back to talks. Trade and jobs in Abkhazia were named a dire need for the folk the war had hurt.

Resolution 1852, adopted on 17 December 2008, covers the final handover in the Hariri murder investigation. The independent commission investigating the 2005 bombing that killed Lebanon's former prime minister had asked for more time. The new Special Tribunal for Lebanon was on track to open at The Hague on 1 March 2009, and Lebanon's prime minister supported the request in a December letter.

The Council extended the commission's mandate until 28 February 2009. The point was continuity: investigators would keep working without a gap while gradually moving operations, staff, and files to The Hague, so the transition finished as the tribunal began. The commission's work on the bombing and other attacks since October 2004 was commended.

Armed groups in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo were still attacking civilians in late 2010. Resolution 1952, adopted on 29 November 2010, renews the sanctions aimed at those groups. The text names the FDLR and the Lord's Resistance Army. Money from illegal mining helped keep such groups armed.

The Council renewed the arms embargo, transport controls, travel bans, and asset freezes until 30 November 2011. It extended the group of experts that monitors the measures. A sixth expert was added to cover natural resources. The text also backed guidelines for companies that buy minerals from Congo. Firms were expected to check their supply chains with care. The aim was to stop the mineral trade from paying for armed groups and abuses.

Resolution 2052, adopted on 27 June 2012, renews the UN Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan Heights. UNDOF watches the area of separation between Israeli and Syrian forces under a 1974 agreement. The Secretary-General reported breaches of that deal, including Syrian troops entering the area in March and shots fired at UN observer teams. Events in Syria's own conflict were starting to spill into UNDOF's zone.

The Council renews UNDOF for six months, until 31 December 2012. It calls on the parties to carry out Resolution 338, respect the 1974 agreement in full, show the greatest restraint, and guard UN staff safety and access. It welcomes work to upgrade the force's gear and sites. A report on events and on steps toward Resolution 338 is due at the end of the period.

Jerusalem's status drew a firm Council line in the spring of 1968. On 21 May, it adopted Resolution 252. Thirteen members voted yes and none voted no. Canada and the United States held back. Israel had seized East Jerusalem in the 1967 war. It was now passing laws the Assembly had already called invalid. Jordan brought the matter back to the Council.

The text restates a core rule: land taken by war cannot be kept. It deplores Israel's failure to heed the Assembly. All Israeli steps that tend to change the city's legal status are declared invalid. Land seizures count among them. Israel must undo such steps and take no more. The Council held this line for decades.

Grenada's application for United Nations membership is the subject of Resolution 352, adopted unanimously on 21 June 1974. The Council had examined the Caribbean island's request, filed as document S/11311. Grenada had become independent from Britain in February of that year, under Prime Minister Eric Gairy.

In its only operative line, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Grenada to membership. Admission resolutions follow a fixed pattern because the Charter allows the Assembly to seat a state only after the Council recommends it. The entry in the record is brief, but it documents the small spice-growing island's formal entry into the community of nations in the mid-1970s.

Israeli settlements in the Arab territories occupied since 1967, including Jerusalem, are taken up in Resolution 452. A commission of the Council had examined the settlements and reported with recommendations. Israel had refused to cooperate with the commission. The resolution was adopted in 1979.

The Council praised the commission's work and accepted its proposals. It said that Israel's policy of building settlements in the occupied lands has no legal validity. The policy breaks the Fourth Geneva Convention, the text holds. The government and people of Israel were called on to stop at once. The building and planning of settlements in those lands, Jerusalem included, had to end. The commission was told to keep watching the situation and report back, given the size of the problem.

Early reports of the United Nations Atomic Energy Commission reached the Council in 1948. The commission had been set up after the Second World War to work on control of atomic energy. It sent its first three reports to the Council. Resolution 52, adopted on 22 June 1948, does one thing with them. It tells the Secretary-General to pass the reports to the General Assembly and to all member states. The record of the Council's own talks on the subject went with them, as a matter of special concern.

Namibia won its independence in March 1990, after decades under South African rule, and it applied to join the United Nations within weeks. Resolution 652 was adopted on 17 April 1990, without a vote against it. The Council examined Namibia's application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that the Republic of Namibia be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation crowned a long campaign, backed by the United Nations for many years, to free the country.
voltaire-micromegas-1752:
Voltaire wrote Micromegas in 1752 as a tale with a sharp point. A giant from a star of Sirius, eight leagues tall, roams the sky. He picks up a small friend from Saturn on his way. The pair come to Earth and at first miss the folk who live here.

With a lens of cut gems they spot a ship full of men of thought. Talk with the small crew shows both pride and true wit in men. The giant laughs at wars fought for specks of mud. The tale is a root work of tales of guests from the stars.
wapping-witch-answer-1652:
Rival prints of the Wapping witch case drew a sharp reply in 1652. A Declaration in Answer to Pamphlets concerning the Witch of Wapping takes the other accounts apart point by point. Such print fights were common, but few over witch cases survive so fully.

The writer charges the first pamphlets with false reports and works to set the record straight. Readers watch two camps argue over what was said, done, and proved. The quarrel shows the witch panic fought out in the press as much as in court. It is a rare, clear look at how trial news was made and unmade.
wapping-witch-relation-1652:
London itself had a witch case in 1652, told in The Witch of Wapping. The pamphlet gives the full relation of the charge and trial in the riverside parish of Wapping. A city case drew eyes that county trials could not.

The text walks readers through the claims, the court work, and the fate of the accused. It brings the hunt for witches to the crowded streets and docks of the capital. Country fears look strange in town dress, and the print knows it. The case shows the panic could touch even the heart of London.
zoist-vol-10-1852:
The Zoist's tenth volume runs from April 1852 to January 1853. A decade of Elliotson's journal now stands in print. Mesmeric practice reports arrive from a loyal band of doctors and amateurs. Trance surgery, once the headline, now shares space with subtler mental cases.

Cerebral physiology still names half the journal's mission on its cover. Somnambulists and their feats draw the curious, as ever. The movement's complete record would fill thirteen volumes by 1856. Volume ten shows a cause grown older, its hopes and habits fixed. What the medical world dismissed, these pages preserved. That preservation is the set's lasting service.
